title: Are the Buffalo Bills really the NFL’s most expensive team to watch live?
summary: A new study conducted by says the Buffalo Bills are now the most expensive team in the NFL to watch in person…I have a problem with that conclusion. Not because attending a Bills game is cheap. It isn’t. Not because tickets for the inaugural season at the new Highmark Stadium aren’t expensive. They absolutely are. […]
full_text: A new study conducted by says the Buffalo Bills are now the most expensive team in the NFL to watch in person…I have a problem with that conclusion. Not because attending a Bills game is cheap. It isn’t. Not because tickets for the inaugural season at the new Highmark Stadium aren’t expensive. They absolutely are. And certainly not because Bills tickets aren’t among the hottest commodities in football right now. They undeniably are. My problem is with what we’re actually measuring and, more importantly, who gets blamed for the number. According to this study from Action Network , the average cost for a family of four to attend a Bills game at the new Highmark Stadium is $2,193.95 when tickets, food, drinks and parking are included. The study analyzed more than 500,000 NFL tickets, with ticket prices sourced through Ticketmaster, and concluded that Buffalo now has the most expensive game-day experience in the league. I’m not buying that, at least not without a lot more context. There’s an important distinction being lost here: First are we including the secondary market in this discussion? Because the price of a Bills season ticket is one thing. A dynamically priced ticket sold directly by an NFL team is another. And the price someone lists that ticket for on the secondary market is something else entirely. Ticketmaster itself explains that resale tickets are priced by the individual reseller and can be listed above or below their original face value. That matters quite a bit when we’re going to crown an NFL ORGANIZATION the “most expensive team to watch”. Because this makes it sound like the Bills are simply pricing out fans. Even Ticketmaster acknowledges NFL ticket prices vary considerably based on the matchup, seat location, date, city, and when the ticket is purchased. So regarding the “average cost” of attending a game, when that snapshot was taken, what inventory was available at that moment, and from whom the ticket was being sourced matters enormously. I paid roughly $650 for a lower-level corner end-zone seat in Atlanta, purchased directly from the Falcons, not on the secondary market. Atlanta is famous for its affordable concessions, and deservedly so, but the cheap hot dog doesn’t help much when you’ve already dropped hundreds of dollars just to get through the gate. For Buffalo’s trip to Las Vegas this season, lower-level tickets directly through the Raiders have been hovering around $750 on average. This isn’t just a Buffalo problem. It’s the NFL ticket market. Especially the Bills. Because they are a premium ticket and have been for the last six-plus seasons no matter where they play and pricing has everything to do with demand. That’s why comparing the cost of a Bills home game against another team’s home game isn’t quite as simple as looking at Ticketmaster on a random summer afternoon and averaging what’s available. The opponent matters. The date matters. The seat matters. And the timing of the purchase matters. A Bills-Chiefs game on Thanksgiving isn’t the same product as a late-season game against a struggling New York Jets. The real story here is the resale market. If we’re talking strictly about resale prices, then there’s a legitimate conversation to have about Buffalo being one of the most expensive NFL experiences right now. No argument from me there. The resale market for the inaugural season at the new stadium has exploded. There is less inventory as the new Highmark Stadium seats roughly 61,000 fans, reducing capacity from the old stadium. There is enormous curiosity surrounding the first season in the building and as per usual there is tremendous demand for Bills tickets. Add to this season-ticket members purchasing Personal Seat Licenses to secure their seats in the new stadium. Those PSLs ranged from hundreds of dollars for some upper-level seats to tens of thousands for premium locations. Do we really think season-ticket holders who paid thousands of dollars for the right to purchase their seats aren’t factoring some of that investment into what they’re willing to accept on resale? Of course they are. Then add the fees associated with buying and selling tickets through the secondary market, and suddenly a ticket that started at one number has grown several new limbs by the time another fan purchases it. That’s the resale market at work. But that isn’t the Bills sitting in a room deciding a family of four should spend more than $2,000 on Sunday afternoon. My season-ticket increase tells a different story. The Bills are still one of the lowest season tickets to own in the NFL. With the move across the street my per-game season-ticket price increased approximately 15% . Would I prefer a zero-percent increase? Of course. But considering the Bills moved into a brand-new $2.1 billion stadium with significantly fewer seats, I actually think the organization did a pretty good job of limiting the increase in the annual ticket price itself. The PSL is another conversation entirely, and I’ve had plenty to say about that. But the PSL and the season-ticket price aren’t the same thing. And can we talk about parking and concessions? I’ve been to 25 of the NFL’s 30 stadiums, and Buffalo isn’t uniquely expensive. Especially when it comes to concessions. They would range right in the middle third of the league in my opinion. And most of us don’t mind a $13 pizza or a $16 basket of tenders and fries as long as it tastes worth it. That has been my argument with the game-day experience in the past. The food at Highmark didn’t match the cost. I’m looking for that to change with better culinary options in the new stadium. There is another place where Buffalo’s game-day culture makes blanket comparisons difficult. You don’t have to park in an official stadium lot. Anyone who has spent a Sunday in Orchard Park knows that parking for a Bills game extends far beyond team-controlled lots. Private lots, businesses, and front yards have been part of Bills game day experience forever. And most of us prefer those options. They’re mostly still within walking distance of the stadium and are substantially cheaper than parking at many NFL venues, with far better tailgating rules, and easier in and out access. The Bills confirm that their controlled lots require advance parking passes, but the surrounding private parking ecosystem remains completely separate from the organization. That’s part of what makes Orchard Park different. Resales of parking passes are going to also be high because there’s a finite number of Bills controlled lots and again with demand and limited supply the prices increase. You can spend a fortune if you want the closest or most convenient option. You can also walk a little farther, hand somebody cash to park in their yard and follow a stream of people wearing Josh Allen jerseys toward the stadium. That isn’t exactly the parking experience surrounding every NFL venue. The new-stadium premium is real, but it won’t last forever There is also something happening in Buffalo right now that can’t be recreated next season. This is the first year. That creates an enormous initial surge in demand. As the season progresses, some of that novelty will wear off. Weather will get colder. Certain opponents will become less attractive. Teams will rise and fall in the standings. Sellers will become more motivated as kickoff approaches. The market will adjust. And by 2027, the new Highmark Stadium won’t be new anymore. I fully expect ticket prices to stabilize once the initial rush of being part of the inaugural season disappears. Expensive? Yes. The NFL’s most expensive organization? That’s a different claim. I don’t normally defend the organization when it comes to financial matters because they get enough of my money, but I felt “bad” for the organization getting any negative attention for something they don’t control. If Action Network’s conclusion is that the current secondary-market cost of taking a family of four to a Bills game is the…

title: What Bills vs. Panthers tells us about actual Buffalo depth chart
summary: Team-released preseason depth charts are mostly nonsense. The teams wouldn’t release them if the league didn’t make them, and what they say is utilized more as PR and internal player motivation that it is anything else. If you really want to know in the preseason how a team views a player, you have to start […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - AUGUST 15: Keon Coleman #0 of the Buffalo Bills makes a catch as Trevin Wallace #32 of the Carolina Panthers makes a tackle during the first half at Highmark Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images Team-released preseason depth charts are mostly nonsense. The teams wouldn’t release them if the league didn’t make them, and what they say is utilized more as PR and internal player motivation that it is anything else. If you really want to know in the preseason how a team views a player, you have to start with the WAWW Factor. When and with whom (WAWW) a player plays in the preseason is far more indicative of their stance on the roster than how a player plays. If a depth cornerback absolutely crushes in in the last quarter of the final preseason game alongside a bunch of players who won’t make the team, his fate is probably already sealed. The fact that he’s playing great is wonderful; the fact that he’s playing in the last quarter of the final preseason game in tandem with other players who likely won’t make the team means he also won’t likely make the team. So what can the WAWW Factor from the preseason game versus the Carolina Panthers tell us about where certain players are located on the Buffalo Bills depth chart, especially at roster battle positions? Ben VanSumeran v Jackson Acker (fullback) As of this writing, the Bills have just released Jackson Acker, meaning if they elect to keep a fullback on the 53 man roster, VanSumeran is the guy. This was clearly reflected in the WAWW Factor for the Bills/Panthers game, with VanSumeran getting every single rep with the starting offensive unit and the first reps with the second offensive unit. Kani Walker v Toriano Pride Jr. (outside CB4) Toriano Pride’s first snap from scrimmage came with 3:15 left in the second quarter. Kani Walker’s first snap from scrimmage came with 1:22 left in the third quarter. Also, Pride played special teams in the first quarter and Walker didn’t play any snaps of teams. Is this because Walker didn’t practice all week? If so, we’ll see a shift in Walker’s usage next preseason game. Knowing that the Walker injury was likely a significant factor in the WAWW Factor we saw in this game, it’d be unwise to draw any firm conclusions. However, if we don’t see a shift in Walker usage when the Bills suit up against the Browns (no teams snaps for Walker, comes in much later in the game compared to Pride Jr.), then it’ll appear that the seventh-round pick has a leg up on the training camp darling. Keon Coleman and Joshua Palmer (WR3) Coleman and Palmer both came in and ran routes with the Bills first team offense, and both of them took their final snap at the beginning of the second quarter. The Bills aren’t currently showing their hand regarding who may actually be WR3 for the team. We’ll keep an eye on it moving forward. Kaleb Elarms-Orr and Dorian Williams (LB2) Kalen Elarms-Orr (KEO) was listed as LB3 on the Bills publicly-released depth chart, and that’s exactly how it played out against the Panthers. Terrel Bernard and Dorian Williams got the first snaps from scrimmage on defense and neither one played in the second half. KEO’s first snap from scrimmage came late in the first quarter and he played into the third quarter. Whether that playing time location changes or not moving forward in the preseason will tell us whether there’s a change KEO takes a starting role as a rookie out of the gate from an veteran or not. Alec Anderson and Austin Corbett (LG) We have an actual competition on our hands, folks. Both Anderson and Corbett got reps with Josh Allen and the other starting offensive linemen. Both played into the second quarter. Neither played in the second half. I would expect Corbett to get the first snaps with the starters when the Bills play the Cleveland Browns next (Anderson got the first ones against Carolina), but even if he doesn’t, the Bills are clearly letting a competition play out based on the WAWW Factor. Sedrick Van-Pran Granger and Lloyd Cushenberry (backup center) Right now, the Bills aren’t behaving like this is a competition. Cushenberry got every snap with Josh Allen in the absence of starter Connor McGovern, and Van-Pran Granger got his first snap with Kyle Allen and continued to play the remainder of the game. Trent Sherfield, Mecole Hardman, and Stephen Gosnell (WR6) We don’t know for sure the Bills will actually keep six wide receivers, but if they do, they didn’t tell us much from the usage against the Panthers. Sherfield played the earliest snaps because he was on the first unit special teams, and all three of them saw their scrimmage usage beginning sometime between the end of the first and the beginning of the second quarter. Ray Davis, not Hardman, was the first player for the team to return a punt. If you made me guess now, I’d take Sherfield in that spot based on teams usage, but nothing about this usage would clearly tip off the team’s current plans. Maxwell Hairston didn’t play, so the “Hairston v IGB” perception of a competition cannot be gauged, though Hairston has gotten far more reps with the starting defense per camp reports. We’ll see if we observe a platoon at CB2 once Hairston is healthy. Ultimately, the line matters more than the dot. These are simply one set of data points that can be used to gauge how the team actually feels about players in competition with each other. The next set of data points will be acquired after the Buffalo Bills play the Cleveland Browns, and we’ll see if anything changes worth noting at that time. …and that’s the way the cookie crumbles. I’m Bruce Nolan with Buffalo Rumblings. You can find me on Twitter and Instagram @BruceExclusive and look for new episodes of “The Bruce Exclusive” every Thursday on the Rumblings Cast Network — see more in my LinkTree!

title: Buffalo Bills 53-man roster projection: After preseason win over Panthers
summary: The Buffalo Bills routed the Panthers 29-14 in the preseason opener, the first outing inside the new Highmark Stadium. With only two more preseason games remaining before the Bills head to Houston to embark on their 2026 regular season, why not project the 53-man roster again? Technically, we do have new information after Buffalo’s opening […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - AUGUST 15: Kyle Trask #14 of the Carolina Panthers runs the ball as Jalon Kilgore #29 of the Buffalo Bills looks to make a tackle during the second half at Highmark Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills routed the Panthers 29-14 in the preseason opener, the first outing inside the new Highmark Stadium. With only two more preseason games remaining before the Bills head to Houston to embark on their 2026 regular season, why not project the 53-man roster again? Technically, we do have new information after Buffalo’s opening exhibition contest. Quarterback (2) Josh Allen Kyle Allen Oscillating back to Kyle Allen as Josh’s backup, as the veteran looked significantly better against the Panthers (14-of-16 for 108 yards) than he did during any point of training camp. Running Back (3) James Cook Ray Davis Ty Johnson Johnson hurt his leg in the Return of the Blue and Red Scrimmage, but it shouldn’t change the numbers game at the running back position for the start of the season. Wide Receiver (7) D.J. Moore Khalil Shakir Josh Palmer Keon Coleman Skyler Bell Mecole Hardman Trent Sherfield Going with seven — instead of what was the traditional six — because this is Joe Brady’s team now, and I assume he’s going to want to pass it and pass it often. Hardman looked as spry as ever at camp, made some plays down the field, and can serve as the club’s primary returner. Sherfield makes it on special teams availability. There weren’t any major developments at this position during the preseason game against the Panthers… beyond Bell sitting out due to injury. Tight End (3) Dalton Kincaid Dawson Knox Jackson Hawes I’ll focus on Hawes here — he played 43% of the offensive snaps as a rookie and turned in a damn good first season in the NFL, particularly for a fifth-round pick. There’s untapped receiving potential in Hawes, and he absolutely has the game to be the stand-in for the departed Reggie Gilliam as a lead-blocking fullback when needed. Offensive Line (9) Dion Dawkins Alec Anderson Connor McGovern O’Cyrus Torrence Spencer Brown Austin Corbett Lloyd Cushenberry Tylan Grable Jude Bowry Flipping from Sedrick Van Pran-Grander a week ago to now Cushenberry as the backup center but keeping 2025 seventh-round pick Chase Lundt as a cut, although it’ll be worth monitoring Tylan Grable’s injury status, because if it lingers that absolutely helps Lundt’s chances to make the team as the swing tackle. Defensive Line (6) * Ed Oliver Deone Walker T.J. Sanders DeWayne Carter Landon Jackson Zane Durant The suspension to Phidarian Mathis absolutely boosts Carter’s chances to make the team, even though he was playing well into the fourth quarter against the Panthers. That’s rarely a good sign for any player attempting to make the team. I’m going with just six (interior) defensive linemen due to a versatile piece I’ll add to another position who can bump inside. Inside Linebacker (4) Terrel Bernard Kaleb Elarms-Orr Dorian Williams Keonta Jenkins This position feels somewhat cemented right now — particularly after a strong performance from Jenkins in the preseason opener. He had two “stops” (tackles that constitute a loss for the offense based on down and distance) without a missed tackle and appeared on 27 snaps. The real question with his position is how does Elarms-Orr fit into the normal rotation during the regular season? Rush Linebacker (6) Greg Rousseau Bradley Chubb Michael Hoecht T.J. Parker Javon Solomon Mike Danna Danna had two sacks — and three total pressures — against backups in the second half, and that was probably to be expected. He was a pesky, dirty-work player for years in Kansas City and has the stocky body type to condense closer to the ball if needed in clear-cut passing situations. He’s a quality insurance option to have for Jim Leonhard’s front. Defensive Backs (10) Christian Benford Maxwell Hairston Dee Alford Davison Igbinosun Cole Bishop CJ Gardner-Johnson Jordan Hancock Jalon Kilgore Kani Walker Sam Franklin Jr. Damar Hamlin will be left out of the projection for now — even though I like to think Leonhard will want a safety with plenty of in-game experience as the primary backup to Gardner-Johnson and Bishop. Here though, the Bills opt for youth, explosiveness, and pure speed over said experience… and Kani Walker makes the club. While not the most ridiculous athlete on the team at corner, he’s an impressive mover at 6’2” and over 200 pounds and did snag that interception against the Panthers, so he gets rewarded for that. Specialists (3) Reid Ferguson Tommy Doman Jr. Tyler Bass I can’t say Doman Jr. clearly won the punter battle in camp, and he didn’t get an opportunity to boot the rock against Carolina but gets the nod as a draft pick over the veteran Mitch Wishnowsky. *Phidarian Mathis will begin serving his three-game suspension at the start of the regular season so he will not originally be on the 53-man roster Week 1.

title: Bills RB James Cook ranked at No. 20 in NFL’s Top 100 Players
summary: It’s not just the Josh Allen Show in Buffalo. James Cook, you know, the Bills running back who led the league in rushing in 2025, is getting his flowers ahead of the 2026 campaign. In the summer-long unveiling of the NFL’s Top 100 Players — as voted on by players themselves, Cook has entered the […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 26: James Cook #4 of the Buffalo Bills runs into the end zone for a touchdown in the third quarter of the game against the Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium on October 26, 2025 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Grant Halverson/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s not just the Josh Allen Show in Buffalo. James Cook, you know, the Bills running back who led the league in rushing in 2025, is getting his flowers ahead of the 2026 campaign. In the summer-long unveiling of the NFL’s Top 100 Players — as voted on by players themselves, Cook has entered the Top 20 No. 20 on the NFL Top 100 Players of 2026… @BuffaloBills RB James Cook! @NFLFilms pic.twitter.com/M6tDPNeOPr — NFL (@NFL) August 17, 2026 Cook is the latest shining example of the Bills’ tremendous developmental system. He didn’t carry the football even 50 times in any of his first three seasons at Georgia. In his final year with the Bulldogs in 2021, when they won the national title, Cook toted the rock 113 times for 728 yards with seven scores on the ground and was the backup to Zamir White who led the team in carries and rushing yards. Despite that, the Bills identified him as a three-down, pass-catching back with serious upside that has now been realized as a professional. He was the third running back off the board — after Breece Hall and Kenneth Walker — in the 2022 NFL Draft. After averaging 5.7 yards per tote in a committee backfield as a rookie, Cook went over 1,100 yards in Year 2, before another 1,000-yard season in 2024 when he averaged 4.9 yards per carry. Last year, as you may very well remember, his 1,621 yards during the regular season were the most among all running backs, and his 1,912 yards from scrimmage were the sixth-most in team history behind two O.J. Simpson seasons in the 1970s and three from Thurman Thomas in the 1990s. And Cook has earned the respect of his peers with the No. 20 ranking in the Top 100 Players list. Dion Dawkins was listed at No. 57. Cook was the fifth running back listed on this year’s Top 100, ahead of Travis Etienne, Kyren Williams, Josh Jacobs, Saquon Barkley, and De’Von Achane. What do you think about Cook’s ranking here? Too high? Too low?
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Josh Allen got more action in preseason game No. 1 than he’s seen in years
summary: Head coach Joe Brady made a promise before the Buffalo Bills’ first preseason game: If a player was healthy, he was playing. I was on record with the assumption that star quarterback Josh Allen was going to come down with a very serious, and very last minute, hangnail. So suffice it to say when I […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - AUGUST 15: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills warms up prior to a preseason game against the Carolina Panthers at Highmark Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images Head coach Joe Brady made a promise before the Buffalo Bills’ first preseason game: If a player was healthy, he was playing. I was on record with the assumption that star quarterback Josh Allen was going to come down with a very serious, and very last minute, hangnail. So suffice it to say when I saw number 17 take to the field on the Bills’ opening possession. A drive that ended with a field goal. “Well” I said, “that’ll be the last we see of Allen today.” But it wasn’t. The starters had one more drive for the day, ending with a Keon Coleman touchdown. As it turns out, it was the most (preseason football) action that Josh Allen has gotten in years. Let’s quantify said “action” Playing time Josh Allen had 15 snaps against the Carolina Panthers, which amounted to 22% of the team’s total snaps. For comparison, Kyle Allen and Shane Buechele had 27 and 25 snaps respectively. So Josh wasn’t exactly featured mind you, but he wasn’t that far behind either. As noted above, this was two drives for Josh Allen. Now there’s no comparison to his 2025 preseason whatsoever. He never played last year until the regular season hit, and you could say he had a good opening night against the Baltimore Ravens. To find the last time Allen played at all, we need to go back to Week 1 of the 2024 preseason, against the Chicago Bears on August 10 of that year. Just over two years since he had ANY preseason play. In that game, Allen had 12% of the team’s playing time, which was only eight snaps. Just over half of what happened this year. When it comes to drives, it was equal to the current year. The starting offense had two drives, they just weren’t very good ones hence the shorter play time. To find a game in which Allen had a greater playing time in the preseason, we need to go back one more year. On August 19, 2023 Josh Allen had 16 snaps against the Pittsburgh Steelers. That was 27% of the team total. Kyle Allen and Matt Barkley had 24 and 20 snaps in that game, respectively. This game was also two drives for Allen, the second long one inflated his snap counts but resulted in a punt. Please note that Allen also played in Week 2 against the Chicago Bears in 2023 as well, just less play time than he did against Pittsburgh (so I’m not looking up any more info on that one). Was Allen put to work? Let’s compare some stats to see if Josh Allen was nominally on the field, or actually getting some warm up reps in. We’ll start with our 2023 game to set our baseline for this one. Against the Steelers that year, Allen was 7 of 10, for 64 yards with zero sacks, touchdowns, or interceptions. That gives us 10 passing downs to six rushing ones for this game. Against the Bears in 2024, Allen was definitely not out there to play. He went two of three. The zero sacks, touchdowns, and interceptions continued in this game as well too. That’s three passes to five rushing downs for the team. In both 2023 and 2024 his longest pass This season, I was pretty shocked at how much Allen threw it around, but was it all that wild statistically. Remember that Allen was on the field for 15 snaps. The last two games had 6.5% passing against Pittsburgh and 37.5% against Chicago. This year, Allen had eight passing attempts and one sack for nine passing downs of 15, or 60% of his playing time. In other words, pretty comparable to 2023’s game against the Steelers, another game where it seems Allen was being asked to get a tune up. For the rest of the stats, Allen had 111 yards, one touchdown, and no interceptions. His longest pass was 32 yards, compared to a long of 15 in both our other games. Allen had a 156.2 passer rating this year. In neither of the other years did Allen even hit 90 in that metric. What does it all even mean? In the grand scheme of things, it merely means that Joe Brady meant what he said; and said what he meant. So far this head coach is faithful… 100% (to his word). It’s possible that with the new scheme-ish on offense, Brady felt it was a good idea to get the team in rhythm with Allen. Or maybe Brady just differs on this philosophically from what Sean McDermott felt was best. Or maybe, just maybe, there was some pressure to have Allen be the first player to hit the field at the new stadium. Heck, if I were Allen I might have even insisted on it. Is there any evidence to this? I’m not sure, but Buffalo did win the coin toss and then they did send Allen out. If only there was some way to deduce their mindset from that and let’s say… the first play called at the new stadium… (14:53) J.Allen pass deep right to K.Shakir to CAR 48 for 21 yards (M.Jackson) Was this Josh Allen's dream scenario to open the stadium? pic.twitter.com/IxuQBKIsmm — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) August 16, 2026

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: cornerback Anthony Kendall
summary: The Buffalo Bills have added some new blood on defense this offseason, especially in the defensive secondary. With defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard set to favor a more man/match-heavy approach when compared with former head coach and defensive boss Sean McDermott’s zone-heavy scheme, it makes sense that new players are needed to fill those roles. Some […]
full_text: Nov 2, 2023; Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA; Tennessee Titans cornerback Anthony Kendall (40) looks on from the sidelines against the Pittsburgh Steelers during the fourth quarter at Acrisure Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Charles LeClaire-USA TODAY Sports | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con The Buffalo Bills have added some new blood on defense this offseason, especially in the defensive secondary. With defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard set to favor a more man/match-heavy approach when compared with former head coach and defensive boss Sean McDermott’s zone-heavy scheme, it makes sense that new players are needed to fill those roles. Some of the players Buffalo added this offseason have clearly defined roles. For example, rookie safety Jalen Kilgore is likely going to make the team and work on special teams, but he will compete for time as a sub-package safety, as well. Other players might have smaller or larger roles depending on their performance in the preseason. In today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days,” we discuss a player whose role is likely just to help the team dress enough players to make it through a preseason game or two. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Anthony Kendall Number: 30 Position: CB Height/Weight: 5’10” 188 lbs. Age: 26 (27 on 12/19/2026) Experience/Draft: 3; signed with the Tennessee Titans following the 2023 NFL Draft College: Baldwin-Wallace Acquired: Signed with Buffalo on 8/12/2026 Financial situation (per OvertheCap): Kendall’s one-year contract is worth $1.075 million, which is the league minimum for a player with his service time. That’s also his cap hit if he makes the 53-man roster. Buffalo can release Kendall at any time without carrying a dead cap charge. 2025 Recap: Kendall spent the 2025 offseason with the Cleveland Browns. He signed with the team in February. However, he did not appear in any preseason games, as he was waived on August 5 with an injury designation. It was a shoulder injury, and it led Kendall to miss the entire 2025 season. He remained a free agent after Cleveland released him. Positional outlook: Kendall is one of nine players listed at cornerback on the current roster. Kani Walker and Maxwell Hairston are dealing with injuries at the moment, but Christian Benford, Dee Alford, Davison Igbinosun, Toriano Pride Jr., Jordan Dunbar, and D.J. Miller are healthy. Te’Cory Couch is listed at defensive back, but he plays corner. Jordan Hancock is also listed at defensive back, and he plays as a hybrid safety/slot corner. 2026 Offseason: Kendall is healthy and he began practicing with Buffalo upon signing. He’s preparing to play in Buffalo’s preseason opener against the Carolina Panthers on August 15. 2026 Season outlook: I hate to sound so negative, but I think it’s more likely that Kendall is released within a few days of Saturday’s preseason contest than it is that he makes the 53-man roster. Perhaps he can show enough to warrant keeping him close, which could lead to a spot on the practice squad, but Buffalo has a host of corners who are more likely to fill roles on both the back end of the roster and the practice squad already in camp. Once they return to full health, Kendall won’t have a place on the squad—again, unless he shows something major in the coming days. Kendall hasn’t played in an NFL game since his rookie season in 2023, and he played almost exclusively on special teams that season. He appeared on 75% of the special teams snaps for the Tennessee Titans, amassing nine special teams tackles on the year. He played just three defensive snaps. He hasn’t even appeared in an exhibition game since the 2024 offseason, so Saturday’s preseason contest is a huge opportunity for him. Kendall’s athletic testing numbers coming out of college were quite good, so perhaps he could come in an surprise everyone in preseason action. He ran a 4.53-second forty-yard dash, and completed the 20-yard shuttle and three-cone drill in 4.44 seconds and 7.02 seconds, respectively. Those numbers don’t jump out, but his 39.5” vertical, 10’9” broad jump, and 19 reps on the bench press at 225 lbs. do. His Relative Athletic Score (RAS) was 8.31, so he clearly has potential based on his athleticism alone. As a former Division III player, Kendall understands the uphill climb he has, and merely by playing in the NFL and joining multiple teams for training camp he’s already done more athletically in his 26 years than I could ever have dreamed of doing in my 40. I wish him luck, but I don’t see a way where he’s with the Bills in September.

title: Panthers roster 2026: Mike Jackson, Rasheed Walker, and Zakee Wheatley are underrated
summary: It was okay that the Carolina Panthers went 8-9 in the 2025 season, because of how they finished. They very nearly beat the Los Angeles Rams in the Wild Card round of the playoffs, in a 34-31 nailbiter that came down to the final 30 seconds. Quarterback Bryce Young was better in the second half […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - NOVEMBER 30: Mike Jackson #2 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates after an interception return touchdown against the Los Angeles Rams during the first quarter at Bank of America Stadium on November 30, 2025 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Grant Halverson/Getty Images) | Getty Images It was okay that the Carolina Panthers went 8-9 in the 2025 season, because of how they finished. They very nearly beat the Los Angeles Rams in the Wild Card round of the playoffs, in a 34-31 nailbiter that came down to the final 30 seconds. Quarterback Bryce Young was better in the second half of the season , no longer looking like the guy head coach Dave Canales had to bench for his own good in 2024. Tetairoa McMillan was the Offensive Rookie of the Year, and the tape showed why — especially when McMillan broke down said tape . A team that had won just seven total games in the 2023 and 2024 seasons looked like a different beast in 2025, and there are reasons to be very encouraged about the future. Signing veteran EDGE Jaelan Phillips to a four-year, $120 million contract was a serious statement, and signing linebacker Devin Lloyd to a three-year, $45 million contract with $25 million guaranteed was another. Yes, there have been unfortunate injuries that could upend things , but it’s easy to put the Panthers in a different competitive tax bracket as the new season begins. If these new Panthers are to work their way up from upstarts to absolutes, they’ll need the best possible work from everybody on the roster — not just the stars, but also those guys whose efforts exceed their national name recognition. To that end, I’ve identified three Hidden Gems for the 2026 Carolina Panthers — one underrated veteran, one underrated free agent, and one underrated draft pick. Underrated veteran: CB Mike Jackson The Seattle Seahawks have a pretty good record of developing defensive backs through the Pete Carroll and Mike Macdonald eras, but anybody can miss one or two. Mike Jackson, who the Dallas Cowboys selected in the fifth round of the 2019 draft out of Miami, passed through Dallas, Detroit, and New England before the Seahawks signed him to their practice squad in 2021. Jackson had two good seasons in Seattle in 2022 and 2023, but in the transition from Carroll to Macdonald, Jackson was traded to the Panthers on August 22, 2024. Dave Canales, who was the Seahawks’ passing game coordinator in 2022, may have had something to do with that. And it was a good thing, because in 2025, Jackson put together his best season to date by far. Last season, the 6’1, 210-pound Jackson allowed 51 catches on 97 targets for 628 yards, 199 yards after the catch, four touchdowns, five interceptions, 17 pass breakups, and an opponent passer rating of 65.1. All season long, Jackson made it clear to opponents that if you wanted to avoid Jaycee Horn and test him instead, you would not generally be happy with the results. The Panthers gave Jackson a two-year, $10 million contract with $5.7 million guaranteed in 2025. They now know that to hold onto him beyond 2026 will cost more than that. “I won’t talk about that part, but I will talk about Mike, just the unbelievable way that he just shows up on a daily basis with focus,” Canales said in his end-of-season presser, when asked about Jackson’s contract status. “He’s an amazing competitor. He’s really brilliant. He’s a heck of a chess player. Our team meals the night before the game and people walk up to the table, and Mike is sitting there and has that gamesmanship about him. He approaches the game that way. Studies film, sick about his craft, technique, footwork. He’s thinking about things, how they may try to attack him in this formation and that. He’s just aware of it all. “The story will be told if you ever saw him in a walkthrough. If you look at his face in a walkthrough, it might as well be the game. His eyes are in the right spot, knees are bent, and he takes it very seriously. That affects the whole group in how we should approach any time we’re on the grass, any time we’re at that meeting. He loves it. Ever since I’ve known him back in Seattle, I remember him running across the field chasing runs down on the backside. I’m talking about practice and camp. I went up to him one day in camp and was like, ‘Mike, you got to be the fittest guy on this team.’ “I just respected so much his work ethic and what he did to pair with his experience and the way he played this year, knocking balls down, coming up with the big interception for us; unbelievable year. I’m just really proud to have been a part of the early story and to watch it progress, and I’m so blessed and fortunate we were able to bring him here last year.” If you want to know how good Jackson can be, watch how he put Davante Adams in several small boxes during Carolina’s 34-31 Wild Card loss to the Los Angeles Rams. Jackson was a primary reason this game was closer than most expected. And keeping him and Horn together should be a primary focus for this franchise. mike jackson vs. davante adams in the playoffs woo doggy @Panthers pic.twitter.com/NnuDZxFUAz — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 13, 2026 Underrated free agent: OT Rasheed Walker Would it be nice for every NFL team to have two future Hall of Fame offensive tackles? Sure. I would also like Brad Pitt’s face, Wright Thompson’s writing chops, and Warren Buffett’s money, please. In lieu of any of that happening, teams often have to do the best they can with what they have when it comes to tackles, especially when injuries set in. The Panthers know all about this, of course. They are currently dealing with injuries to left tackle Ikem Ekwonu and right tackle Taylor Moton, which leaves them with the placements of first-round pick Monroe Freeling and veteran Rasheed Walker, the former Green Bay Packer who signed a one-year, $4 million contract with $3.215 million guaranteed. The money tells you that this was a depth signing, as opposed to an estimation that Walker would man one side of the line all season long, but that could indeed happen. Last season for the Packers, Walker allowed five sacks, three quarterback hits, and 33 quarterback hurries as the full-time left tackle. It was the third straight season he filled that role for Matt LaFleur’s team, ever since Walker replaced an injured David Bakhtiari in Week 2 of the 2023 season. The 2022 seventh-round pick out of Penn State has never been a top-tier tackle, but he’s consistent enough to maintain his stature in an offense without everything falling apart. “Just one day at a time, just being able to challenge the group to bring out the best in the group,” Canales said in late July about what Walker brings to the front five. “Without getting into any specifics, I’m just excited that we have a veteran guy that can just create a level of comfort, as you can imagine, for the quarterback on that left side. He knows what he’s doing. He’s been around it all. He’s seen it all, and as we have different guys popping in at guard, it’s really nice to just have that piece there. He has a lot of great energy. There are things I didn’t know about him and his personality, he enjoys it. He celebrates stuff even when he’s not in and there’s a big play on the offense, the first one with his hands in the air. Love that about him. Love that he’s bringing that kind of veteran leadership.” So no, Walker isn’t going to race to the Pro Bowl unless some surprising things happen in 2026, but that’s not the point. When you can avail yourself of an NFL starting tackle even after your depth chart at the positions have taken some serious hits, there’s nothing at all wrong with that. And in an NFL where guys like Dan Moore Jr. and Jawaan Taylor are cashing $20 million checks every year when they’re below league-average? All in all, the Walker signing could be one of the smartest things the Panthers did this offseason. Rasheed Walker isn't the next Trent Williams or anything, but…

summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener for at least the past ten years. full_text: 14 Nov 1999: Steve Beuerlein #7 of the Carolina Panthers calls the count from the line of scrimmage during the game against the St. Louis Rams at the Trans World Dome in St. Louis, Missouri. The Rams defeated the Panthers 35-10. Mandatory Credit: Elsa Hasch /Allsport | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #27. Steve Beuerlein Panthers stats: 59 games, 12,690 passing yards, 86 TDs, 50 INT, 60.4% completions , 1X Pro Bowl Career stats: 147 games, 24,046 passing yards, 147 TDs, 112 INT, 56.9% completions , 1X Pro Bowl Quarterback Steve Beuerlein played five solid seasons for the Panthers from 1996, Carolina’s second season as a new franchise, through 2000. The Panthers entered the NFL as a brand new franchise back in 1995 and surprised many by going a respectable 7-9 in their debut season behind rookie quarterback Kerry Collins. As the Panthers entered their 1996 season they wisely decided to invest in a veteran signal caller behind Collins, and they rode with Steve Beuerlein. Before joining the Panthers as a 31-year-old journeyman, Beuerlein began his professional career in 1987 as a fourth round pick by the Raiders. He spent two seasons there as a spot starter then began what would become a nomadic life in the NFL. After the Raiders he played two seasons with the Dallas Cowboys, seeing the field only sparingly. The next two seasons were spent with the Cardinals where he was the team’s starting quarterback in 1993, throwing for 3,164 yards with 18 touchdowns and 17 interceptions. He then spent 1995 as a spot starter for the Jacksonville Jaguars in his age-30 season. When the Panthers came calling in 1996, it looked like yet another backup job for the former Notre Dame star. After all, Kerry Collins, the No. 5 pick in the 1995 draft, was the team’s young franchise quarterback. Unless Collins got hurt or ran into problems off the field, Beuerlein would mostly be holding a clipboard in Charlotte. And, yes, Collins would deal with both injuries and off-the-field issues , which opened the door for the veteran Beuerlein to regularly see the field for the Panthers. In 1996 Beuerlein appeared in eight games with four starts for a 12-4 Panthers squad that lost in the conference championship game, throwing for 879 yards with eight touchdowns and two interceptions. In 1997 he was once again called upon to fill in for Collins. Beuerlein appeared in seven games, starting three, with 1,032 yards, six touchdowns, and three picks. By 1998 the Panthers were ready to move on from Kerry Collins after he benched himself with the team’s 0-4 start and turned the reins over to a now 33-year-old Steve Beuerlein. He started all 12 games in which he appeared with a 4-8 quarterback record, but he threw for 2,613 yards with 17 touchdowns and 12 interceptions. That year his 63.0% completion percentage led the NFL . In 1999 everything came together for the 34-year-old journeyman. He led the Panthers to an 8-8 record and his 4,436 passing yards led the NFL. His 36 passing touchdowns ranked second in the NFL and he also finished second in passer rating. In 1999 he earned his first and only Pro Bowl nod. In 2000 he once again started all 16 games for the Panthers, but took a step back statistically. Carolina went 7-9. His 3,730 passing yards dipped more than 700 yards from his Pro Bowl season. His touchdowns plummeted from 36 to 19 while his interceptions rose from 15 t0 18. Carolina released Beuerlein before their disastrous 1-15 2001 campaign. Beuerlein continued his career post-Panthers by playing sparingly for the Broncos in 2002 and 2003 before calling it a career. Steve Beuerlein is deserving of such a lofty position on our Top 100 countdown because of what he did for the Panthers. He offered a veteran’s stability, maturity, and excellence as Kerry Collins dealt with his health and personal issues. The Panthers 1998 season was tumultuous with Collins, as some have said, “quitting” on his team four games into the season. Fortunately, the Panthers had Steve Beuerlein to fill the void. He helped the Panthers keep their heads above water and play at least competent football. Individually, once thrust into the starting role he put together back-t0-back seasons as one of the most consistent, efficient quarterbacks in the league. He deserved his 1999 Pro Bowl honors, just as he deserves the No. 27 spot on our Top 100 list.

summary: For the entirety of the offseason the Chicago Bears largely stood pat with their defensive line. As first reported by Matt Zenitz of CBS Sports, and now officially announced by the team, the Bears […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - SEPTEMBER 22: Marcus Davenport #92 of the Detroit Lions reac during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game between the Arizona Cardinals and the Detroit Lions at State Farm Stadium on September 22, 2024 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images For the entirety of the offseason the Chicago Bears largely stood pat with their defensive line. Today brings an entirely new face to the lineup as well as a reunion between a veteran and his former coach. As first reported by Matt Zenitz of CBS Sports , and now officially announced by the team, the Bears have signed defensive end Marcus Davenport. The official terms of the deal are not known to be finalized as of the writing of this article. This is also his 3rd different team in the last five years. He most recently played for the Detroit Lions from 2024 through 2025. Let’s get the pink elephant out of the way first. He’s played in only 14 games since signing his 1-year $13M deal with the Minnesota Vikings in 2023 due to injuries. That is a far cry from his 63 career appearances while with Dennis Allen and the New Orleans Saints from 2018 until 2022. He was a completely different player under Allen than anywhere else he’s been in the league. That includes registering a respectable 21.5 sacks in 5 years with Allen — and a career best 9.0 in 2021 — along with 95 pressures following his selection at 14th overall during the 2018 NFL Draft. It remains to be seen how much the 8-year veteran has left in the tank. This is the first “notable” move the Bears have made at defensive end to this date. Whether or not more changes are on the way remains to be seen.

summary: The Chicago Bears have long struggled to maintain a quality offensive line, but under Ben Johnson there seems to be a true push to have quality starters and meaningful depth throughout the line. However, it’s not enough to simply have names, those names have to be attached to players who can answer the bell. Every […]
full_text: Chicago Bears center Logan Jones (54) sets the ball before a play in the second quarter of a preseason game against the Cleveland Browns on Saturday, Aug. 15, 2026, at Soldier Field in Chicago. (John J. Kim/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) The Chicago Bears have long struggled to maintain a quality offensive line, but under Ben Johnson there seems to be a true push to have quality starters and meaningful depth throughout the line. However, it’s not enough to simply have names, those names have to be attached to players who can answer the bell. Every year, I use preseason to familiarize myself with the depth of the team. This is not a comprehensive breakdown of every player and every snap. Instead, this is a loose summary and evaluation of the notes I took watching the play of the offensive line three or four times (more on individual snaps if a lot was going on and I wanted to dial in). Also, although this is an assessment of the offensive line, I have to shout out Kaden Davis, who had some of the best blocking I’ve seen from a wide receiver in a preseason game in a long time. He was energetic, targeted, and structurally sound in his technique. For each player I tried to assess his general level of play and commented on strengths and weaknesses, concluding with the maximum level of reliance I would be comfortable with for the player in question, followed by relevant context from their career to date. For a frame of reference, I have included a similar summary of my notes that I took on Ozzy Trapilo from last season. Ozzy Trapilo (#75) Overview: As the season progressed, Trapilo showed a capable understanding of kickstep, slide, and stutter timing, reaching mid-tier starter level by the end of the season. His understanding of blocking evolution was on par with other starting tackles. He was enthusiastic in the run game, and his starting pad level was adequate there. His single best move was a latch followed by upward pressure using his length, which he used to mitigate who transitioned speed to power and against lesser defenders where it helped him win the rep outright. At his best, Trapilo used awareness, angle, and size against defenders who engaged poorly, especially when he could play within himself athletically. Even when overwhelmed by outside speed, he was seldom sucked into overcommitting, and he found a partial answer for interior speed with improved technique. Concerns: Unfortunately, he was clingy instead of offering a true punch or jolt, and he never really enforced his will in pass protection, allowing defenders to force him back prematurely. When facing inside speed, he aspired to neutral play instead of plus play, and struggled consistently against low outside speed. His adjustments in run blocking were not instinctual, yet, and he lost time trying to adjust to shifting fronts, losing leverage due to inferior body alignment. When stymied, he tended to lean and reach a lot. He narrowed too readily while run-blocking, letting his ankles slide close. His pad level often degraded by the fourth quarter, and he did not have the raw athleticism to make up for this lack of conditioning. He was unable to match power with the big dogs and he did not have an offsetting advantage in speed or timing. Defenders with a full toolkit found weaknesses in his game, even if he proved himself as a plausible long-term starter prior to injury. Maximum comfort level: If fully recovered, I would be comfortable with him as the starting left tackle for the season. Other notes: Ranked 37/89 among offensive tackles by PFF, with a 3.4% blown block rate per Sports Info Solutions. He has 563 regular-season snaps, with 490 of those on offense instead of special teams. Theo Benedet (#79) Overview: Benedet played like a starting-level or high-reserve offensive tackle in the NFL. Essentially an ideal swing tackle, he displayed an ability to shut down inside leverage and maintained clean position throughout. He showed an ability to drive his man off the ball, he stayed low and handled outside speed reliably, and he was able to keep his hips and shoulders targeted downfield. When he lost, it was typically to inside speed or a combination of power and leverage. However, he is clearly a competent player. Maximum comfort level: I’d be comfortable with him protecting Caleb in a divisional game if the rest of the line consisted of starters. Other notes : Rated 72/89 among qualifying offensive tackles by PFF with a 6.1% blown block rate per Sports Info Solutions. He has 649 regular-season snaps, with 577 on offense. Logan Jones (#54) Overview: One of the best things to say about a rookie offensive lineman is that he was boring, and Logan Jones was boring for most of his reps. He sank his pad level to a good height, and he consistently aligned his hips with his target, using the beginning of a punch to create distance. In the run, he would regularly climb to the second level and drive through his man, finishing the play with aggression. He was able to provide an actual “hard jam” against lighter defenders, and was variously able to handle simple bullrushes and unsophisticated uses of speed. There was at least one rep where he took a defender’s balance with timing and leverage, even if it was not a true pancake. At times, he was also able to drive through his man in pass protection as well, and he displayed awareness of play evolution at a basic level, sometimes mitigating the mistakes of others on the line with his own reactions and adjustments. He also adjusted to his own mistakes well. Of note, he reacted rapidly to the offsides, the interception, and being left outnumbered, showing a sound ‘offensive computer’ instead of relying on expectation. While he did not play at a veteran level, he played with good awareness for a rookie. Concerns: He had a few hard losses to outside power, and while he attempted to re-engage and establish himself, or to mitigate the loss by guiding and pressing, these were clear losses. Additionally, on some of his run game reps he was content to win against his man slowly instead of with the urgency to allow the runner a cleaner lane. He would get tied up and not keep his feet active, preventing play progression. Maximum comfort level: I’d be comfortable with him blocking for Swift or Monangai on 4th-and-2 to seal a game in-conference. Other notes: PFF had him 9/309 qualified college centers in 2025. Kiran Amegadjie (#72) Overview: He has fairly light feet, and when he is able to backpedal cleanly he maintains good timing and distance. A few times he was able to keep his man in front of him, hips squared and shoulders low enough to provide a simple sort of drive with clean, efficient steps. He was tenacious, seldom giving up on plays completely, re-engaging after the first loss eagerly. Very, very few tackles have as stable foot placement as he does when it gets “muddy” around them. In some ways, his style of play made him seem better suited to moving inside to guard rather than staying at tackle, because he plays worse when he has extra space around him and his footwork leaves him able to handle inside traffic, but he lacks the capacity to handle power or leverage in the manner an inside move would require. Concerns: However, he lets his feet get overly narrow and he does not use his feet to open space or to maintain leverage, simply to not lose angle. He readily overcorrects on his kick slide and he will “over eat” space when he is trying to mirror, causing the pocket to restrict unnecessarily. He will blindly concede space even when it isn’t necessary, just for the sake of moving his feet. He will stand too tall and guide defenders around him and into the main action instead of dropping his pads, leaning in, and delivering power or resistance. He readily overreaches and gets grabby, clutching instead of driving or punching. On different reps he quickly lost to outside leverage, outside speed, and any power. He showed no…

title: An Odyssey for Beef on Chicago’s Defensive Line
summary: Throughout the entire offseason and preseason, there have been countless stories about the Chicago Bears and the state of their defensive line. Earlier in the spring came news and confirmation that general manager Ryan Poles inquired about Las Vegas Raiders All-Pro defensive end Maxx Crosby. Shortly thereafter came speculation on Arizona Cardinals Pro Bowl EDGE […]
full_text: Aug 6, 2026; Tampa, FL, USA; Tampa Bay Buccaneers defensive tackle Vita Vea (50) looks on during training camp at AdventHealth Training Center. Mandatory Credit: Nathan Ray Seebeck-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Throughout the entire offseason and preseason, there have been countless stories about the Chicago Bears and the state of their defensive line. Earlier in the spring came news and confirmation that general manager Ryan Poles inquired about Las Vegas Raiders All-Pro defensive end Maxx Crosby. Shortly thereafter came speculation on Arizona Cardinals Pro Bowl EDGE Josh Sweat following his formal trade request. Most recently came news the Bears have checked in on Tampa Bay Buccaneers defensive tackle Vita Vea . No matter how you slice it, the dots all connect towards the same destination – a major swing being prepared to bolster the trenches on defense. And yet, despite their defensive line being perhaps their biggest position of need, we haven’t seen much action being taken. Whether it has been due to asking price, fit, or a combination of the two; we have yet to see such a transaction take place. At least up to the writing of this article. Today I am examining each of those three distinct possibilities and breaking down just how well the previously mentioned players fit into the Bears’ end goal of hoisting the Vince Lombardi Trophy. All three share similarities as well as differences to consider. OLB Maxx Crosby You read that headline correctly, as “Mad Maxx” is listed as a “WILL” LB on the depth chart for the Las Vegas Raiders. It will be a career first for Crosby as he’s played exclusively within 4-man fronts dating back to his days in college at Eastern Michigan. The Eastern Michigan Eagles ran a derivative of the 4-2-5 front, and then both Paul Gunther (2019-2021) as well as Patrick Graham (2022-2025) had their own spins on 4-3 under concepts during their respective times as defensive coordinators for the Raiders. While base fronts rarely crack more than 30% of a team’s total lineup on defense, this is still a significant consideration to make. We also don’t need to rehash the entire trade debacle which took place earlier this offseason. Instead, the point needs to be made that the Raiders made the decision to move on from Maxx Crosby once already. They can just as easily make that same decision again and have built their roster accordingly. The only reason he’s still in Las Vegas is because the Baltimore Ravens developed cold feet (I’m calling it as I see it) and backed out. The Raiders have until November’s trade deadline to find a new partner. I’d imagine general manager John Spytek is holding out for a deal which matches what he was originally promised. There’s really no question whatsoever as to how good Maxx Crosby would fit within the Bears’ defense. He’d resume his usual duties as a defensive end adjacent from Montez Sweat, which would form one of the better pass rush tandems in the league. Crosby’s arrival would also go a long ways to beefing up Chicago’s unit against the run. Maxx Crosby the run stuffer is almost as elite as Maxx Crosby the pass rusher. Per PFF, he ranked 2nd in stops with 46 and 1st among defensive ends in snaps against the run (410). What might be the showstopper is his recent injury history. That failed physical (torn and repaired meniscus) with the Ravens has been questioned a great deal by people from around the league, yet it will still be part of his medical record for when teams resume trade negotiations for Maxx. On this subject, it has been made clear Ryan Poles does not take medical evaluations lightly and will not take a major medical risk unless he’s assured the player will be available to contribute. Dating back to the spring, the Bears were interested in Maxx Crosby and did have conversations about the prospects of a trade before the Raiders took the Ravens’ offer of two whole 1st-round picks. It is unknown what Ryan Poles’ final price is and he’s operated with his self-made mandate of not deviating from his bottom-line offer. The question remains – just how interested is Ryan Poles in re-engaging a potential deal down the road? EDGE Josh Sweat The amount of interest in Josh Sweat has been a bit of a mystery ever since the Pro Bowler and his agent formally submitted their request for a trade following the firing of Jonathan Gannon as their head coach. While he’s nowhere near as big a splash as any potential deal for Maxx Crosby, Josh Sweat is a damn good player in his own right. He also offers a bit more flexibility in how he can be used up front on defense. I rarely use the term “EDGE” when writing about football, as both defensive end and outside linebacker are distinctly different positions and recognized as such in the NFL. However, in the case of Josh Sweat, he has played both positions during his time with the Philadelphia Eagles and Arizona Cardinals. There’s been no drop-off in his production while playing in any alignment as well. As of this moment, he is still listed on the PUP list for an unspecified knee injury. Otherwise, he has been healthy for a vast majority of his NFL career. What most people will point out is his good, not great, production as a pass rusher. Sacks aren’t everything, but he’s had just two seasons where he cracked double digits in this statistic. In fact he’s been pretty comparable to Chicago’s Montez Sweat, particularly in pressures registered. Which is by no means a bad thing, just an observation between two rock-solid players. Both players have been the primary pass-rushing threat for their respective teams these last few years. When you truly think about this possibility, it almost makes the most sense for the Bears in terms of fit and price. His contract isn’t small but definitely is manageable and can be made a point of emphasis in any potential trade offer. I.E. the more money the Bears try to take on, of which they don’t really have much available in the first place, the lower the value of the draft pick(s). The opposite is true as well. For what it’s worth, there is an out built into Josh Sweat’s deal for 2027 as well. On paper, Josh fits in as an ideal partner adjacent to Montez Sweat on the field just as much as it would be a marketing opportunity for Old Spice. DT Vita Vea Of the trio, Vita Vea is the first and only true defensive tackle the Bears might be assessing as a trade target. While the Tampa Bay Buccaneers have been adamant about not shopping their stud nose tackle, tangible reports have linked the Bears as a potential suitor and trade partner. Vita’s arrival would not just be massive in the literal sense. He would transform the Bears’ defensive line from the interior-on-out. That might be the first argument to have – which position group between defensive end and tackle needs more help right now? And, after considering both Vita Vea’s current prospects and the potential impact Dexter Lawrence could have made, I’m leaning towards tackle. Here is why. Aside from rookie Jordan van den Berg, no players have contracts lasting past 2027. Grady Jarrett’s deal has an optional out built in to exercise for 2027, which is the same for Neville Gallimore, and everyone else, including Gervon Dexter Sr’s contracts, will expire at season’s end this year. By comparison, there’s more certainty at the end between players like Montez Sweat and Austin Booker. Before we get too carried away, we have to remember why Vita Vea and his agency requested a trade recently. They want a (well-earned) pay raise, plain and simple. His $18M average has fallen considerably compared to his peers thanks to a slew of big contract extensions for even bigger men. He’s also one of only two true nose tackles in the league who have posted elite numbers against both the run and the pass rush. We were all amazed by the numbers posted for Dexter Lawrence prior to his sign-and-trade deal between the Cincinnati Bengals and New York Giants. Who was the second player ranked…

title: Which Bengals rookie has impressed you the most so far?
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals have now completed the bulk of training camp, as well as their first preseason game, which has given us plenty of opportunities to see the 2026 rookie class in action. Overall, it’s been a good showing for the news kids on the block, including several game-changing plays made in the 16-14 preseason […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - AUGUST 13: Wide receiver Colbie Young #86 of the Cincinnati Bengals in a preseason game between the Detroit Lions and the Cincinnati Bengals on August 13, 2026, at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati, OH. (Photo by Jeff Moreland/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals have now completed the bulk of training camp, as well as their first preseason game, which has given us plenty of opportunities to see the 2026 rookie class in action. Overall, it’s been a good showing for the news kids on the block, including several game-changing plays made in the 16-14 preseason win over the Detroit Lions. Seventh-round tight end Jack Endries scored his first NFL touchdown while catching a game-high-tying three passes for 25 yards. He even earned a game-high 91.4 Pro Football Focus grade . Second-round edge Cashius Howell didn’t make quite as much noise as he did in camp, though he still managed to get one QB hurry and recovered a fumble in a game decided by just two points. Seventh-round defensive tackle Landon Robinson managed to pick up his first NFL sack to go with another QB hit. And then there’s fourth-round wide receiver Colbie Young, who has put on a show in camp and managed to haul in two passes for 28 yards against Detroit. full_text: TAMPA, FL - AUGUST 06: Tampa Bay Buccaneers Wide Receiver Emeka Egbuka (2) goes thru drills during Training Camp on August 06, 2026 at the AdventHealth Training Center at One Buccaneer Place in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Cliff Welch/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images We are less than a month away from the Cincinnati Bengals opening the season against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. As teams continue their training camps and preseason schedule, all eyes will soon turn to the games that count, and for these two teams, that date is September 13th. The Bengals have been relatively lucky on the injury front this training camp, aside from the uncertainty surrounding Shemar Stewart’s hyperextended knee. Per a report on Monday, though, Tampa Bay could be without one of their star players. Second-year wide receiver Emeka Egbuka is dealing with a toe injury that has his status in doubt for Week 1. Todd Bowles said Emeka Egbuka is “day-to-day, week-to-week” with a toe sprain. When asked if it could affect Week 1 availability, Bowles said he could not say at this time. pic.twitter.com/lyt3yMCSyD — Evan Closky (@ECloskyWTSP) August 17, 2026 While head coach Todd Bowles didn’t rule Egbuka out, he sounded less than certain that their star receiver will be ready to go for Week 1. Egbuka had 938 yards and six touchdowns last season, and with Mike Evans now with the San Francisco 49ers, Egbuka will likely be their top receiving option going forward. Obviously, you never want to see players missing games for injury, but if Egbuka can’t suit up to start the season, that likely changes the Bengals’ defensive game plan quite a bit.

title: ESPN’s Mina Kimes and Ben Solak predict Joe Burrow will win MVP
summary: As successful as he’s been in Cincinnati, Joe Burrow has yet to reach his full potential. Part of that is due to injuries. Part of that is due to terrible offensive lines. And part of that is due to poor defensive play the last couple of years. Now that all three of those issues seem […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - AUGUST 13: Joe Burrow #9 of the Cincinnati Bengals warms up prior to a game against the Detroit Lions at Paycor Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images As successful as he’s been in Cincinnati, Joe Burrow has yet to reach his full potential. Part of that is due to injuries. Part of that is due to terrible offensive lines. And part of that is due to poor defensive play the last couple of years. Now that all three of those issues seem to be resolved, we’re seeing some of the smartest football analysts predicting that Joe Burrow will win MVP for the first time in his career. ESPN’s Mina Kimes told guest Ben Solak on her podcast that she chose Burrow to win MVP over Justin Herbert in part because the growth of the latter this year could largely be attributed to new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel. “My feeling about Burrow was this—one, he’s never won it,” Kimes began. She then talked about how highly regarded Burrow is by other analysts. “I just feel that, everything is in place. There’s no contract drama with the wide receivers.” Kimes thinks Burrow has a real chance because this year he has a “sneaky decent” offensive line and the 32nd-ranked schedule, according to the FTN Fantasy Almanac. Solak agreed, saying the MVP is a “narrative-driven award” and Burrow has never won it. He also said that the Bengals’ improvement this year will be attributed to the QB who has “many, many years toiling away at the helm,” and not Al Golden, Scott Peters, Dylan Fairchild, or other less prominent faces. title: Bengals News: Jeff Blake breaks down Joe Burrow
summary: Former Cincinnati Bengal quarterback Jeff Blake attended practice recently. He had a very good breakdown of Joe Burrow’s game while also making a prediction most fans are hoping for as well. “He’s got a tight throwing motion, really good mechanics, generates a lot of power in his throws, and he’s really accurate,” Blake told Dan […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - DECEMBER 11: Jeff Blake #8 of the Cincinnati Bengals looks to pass against the New York Giants during an NFL football game December 11, 1994 at Giants Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. Blake played for the Bengals from 1994-99. (Photo by Focus on Sport/Getty Images) | Getty Images Former Cincinnati Bengal quarterback Jeff Blake attended practice recently. He had a very good breakdown of Joe Burrow’s game while also making a prediction most fans are hoping for as well. “He’s got a tight throwing motion, really good mechanics, generates a lot of power in his throws, and he’s really accurate,” Blake told Dan Hoard . “He was blessed to have the opportunity to take this team to a Super Bowl, and he’s young enough to do it again.” Blake may not be the first quarterback to come to mind when you think of Cincinnati quarterbacks who have had long stints with the team, but he is currently help this younger generation of quarterbacks reach their full potential as the Director of quarterback academy at IMG. He breaks down the fundamentals for a living. It is always good to hear from a former fan favorite about these current Bengals. Bengals News Five Observations from Day 12 of Bengals Training Camp “I knew my time would come if I was just patient,” Hudson said. “There’s no point in being uptight about it or getting mad about it, your time is going to come and you’re either prepared to make a play or you’re not.” The tight end room is quietly getting pretty crowded. Tanner Hudson has survived Roster’ cuts so far, but things are getting close with young players like Erick All, Jack Endries and Cam Grandy. Not to mention Mike Gesicki and Drew Sample are both veteran players who have played a ton of snaps for this team already. Training Camp Report | Joe Burrow Tames The Dog Days With Icy Execution “As soon as I get out of my break, the ball is there. Like I’ve said, you can’t guard a perfect ball,” Young said. “Just me and Joe trusting each other on that timing route. He makes it easy. All that pressure in his face, he has to read all the checks, and he still threw a perfect ball out there.” The more you hear from Colbie Young the more he sounds like he understands the multiple levels of the offense and defense beyond what a normal receiver might. It shows up in just how often we have seen him makes plays time and time again so far in training camp. Bengals rookie Ceyair Wright bolts camp for big movie role “We wish him the best. He was fun to be around, he really competed hard for us. It was fun watching him play,” Taylor said. “But obviously he’s chosen to go a different path.” Just when you think you have seen it all you are reminded why the NFL is just an unbelievable reality TV show writers wished they could script. I mean this guy was in the new Space Jam, so it isn’t hard to believe he might be headed for bigger things as an actor than as an undrafted free agent trying to make a team. How the preseason opener instantly defined Bengals’ new identity Things were looking pretty hairy around this time last year. Yes, Burrow was healthy throughout training camp, but Trey Hendrickson’s contract situation was like a dark cloud that indeed foreshadowed an ominous 2025 campaign for the defense. It is nice going into a season without the latest player hold-in weighing on everything the team is doing. There seems to be an air of optimism as the front office seems to have finally taken their version of a big swing. NFL News Cowboys agree to terms with eight-time Pro Bowl pass rusher Von Miller He’s the current active leader in career sacks with 138.5, having racked up nine last year to lead the Commanders despite starting only three of 17 games. That number was the most since a 9.5-sack effort combined between the Broncos and Rams in 2021, a year that divides Miller’s career quite cleanly. Teams hoping to make that push to being a contender are starting those mid-training cap additions. Maybe I is time to get a veteran linebacker in the fold for Cincinnati. Report: Cardinals RB Jeremiyah Love unlikely to play again in preseason due to high ankle sprain Love is dealing with a high ankle sprain and is unlikely to play again this preseason, ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported Sunday. Schefter added that the team is hopeful the No. 3 overall pick can return for the regular-season opener on Sept. 13 against the Chargers. It is best to be safe, but it was nice to see such a talented rookie get an opportunity to shine before the regular season. Rams’ Sean McVay has no timeline for Aaron Donald decision: ‘I am hopeful that it will be sooner rather than later’ “Here’s what I would say; we have a great dialog,” McVay said Saturday night, via team transcript. “It’s going to be on his timeline. When he feels good about having clarity, whether that is yes or whether that ends up being a no, we have had some tentative decisions behind the scenes.” Another contender level team hoping to build one of the more dynamic one-two punches from pass rushers ever seen by adding Donald to Myles Garrett on their defensive line.

title: Dexter Lawrence knows what his job is with the Bengals
summary: It’s not just Dexter Lawrence being a great football player that makes it clear why the Bengals made the bold move to trade for him in mid-April. Lawrence is an incredible leader, and he is very confident and secure in himself. He knows what his role needs to be with the Bengals. If you need […]
full_text: Aug 13, 2026; Cincinnati, Ohio, USA; Cincinnati Bengals defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence II (97) runs onto the field before the game against the Detroit Lions at Paycor Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Katie Stratman-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect It’s not just Dexter Lawrence being a great football player that makes it clear why the Bengals made the bold move to trade for him in mid-April. Lawrence is an incredible leader, and he is very confident and secure in himself. He knows what his role needs to be with the Bengals. If you need proof of all of this, listen to two interviews with him that aired on the Bengals Preseason TV Network Thursday night in the Bengals’ win over the Detroit Lions. Lawrence did an interview with the Voice of the Bengals, Dan Hoard, back in April, and Thursday night he spoke with Bengals Preseason TV Network sideline reporter, Joe Danneman. Both interviews, aired Thursday night, show the kind of player and leader the Bengals have on their defensive line and defense overall. Or, take this interview he did recently on SiriusXM NFL Radio. "My job is to make everybody's job around me easier." @Bengals DT Dexter Lawrence discussed his role in the Cincinnati defense. 📻 https://t.co/1S6vayaSYT #Bengals | #WhoDey | @SolomonsWisdom | @DLInTheTrenches pic.twitter.com/w3wLW4RA04 — SiriusXM NFL Radio (@SiriusXMNFL) August 10, 2026 Here’s how I interpret that quote. Lawrence understands his role, but that doesn’t mean taking a back seat when it comes to individual stats. Lawrence stuffing his individual stat sheet probably means other players on the defensive line are also getting theirs, or making impacts in lesser-glorified stats. With Lawrence clogging the middle, that’s going to enable Boye Mafe, Myles Murphy, Cashius Howell, and Myles Murphy to collapse the pocket off the edge. Pressures can make a big enough impact, especially if they allow the interior defensive linemen to finish at the quarterback. The excitement is building for the regular-season opener on September 13th against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. If Lawrence gets a sack in that game, it’s very likely he’ll be hitting the Sexy Dexy dance in The Jungle.
