title: Experts weigh in on Detroit Lions preseason debuts of Blake Miller, Seth McLaughlin
summary: The Detroit Lions didn’t play most of their starters against the Cincinnati Bengals on Thursday, but there were a few very important players in action. First-round pick Blake Miller played for the entire first half. The Lions’ projected starting right tackle has had an up-and-down camp, which is to be expected when he’s lining up […]
full_text: Detroit Lions tackle Blake Miller (76) practices during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions didn’t play most of their starters against the Cincinnati Bengals on Thursday, but there were a few very important players in action. First-round pick Blake Miller played for the entire first half. The Lions’ projected starting right tackle has had an up-and-down camp, which is to be expected when he’s lining up against Aidan Hutchinson. Lions coach Dan Campbell thought it was important to douse the rookie in as many reps as possible to get him ready for Week 1 of the regular season. “It’s a work in progress, and I think a lot of it right now is the pass protection,” Campbell said last week. “I like the run game, but it’s really – it’s the whole game. But listen, he’s in a good spot. And we are going to douse him with reps. We are going to find a way and he will find a way to be the guy.” So how did Miller do in his first NFL action? Well, PFF gave him a 66.6 overall grade, which ranked 55th among 166 offensive tackles in action this past weekend. They credited him with two pressures allowed in 24 pass blocking reps, resulting in a 68.1 pass blocking grade. But let’s throw PFF to the side for a minute. What do true offensive experts think of Miller’s performance? Thankfully, a few weighed in on social media. First, there’s Geoff Schwartz, who played eight seasons in the NFL as an offensive lineman. He put together a cut-up of Miller’s night, and had some high praise for the rookie right tackle. Small sampling of Blake Miller last night. Pass pro looked clean. Moved feet well. Good strikes. Mixed up pass sets which I loved. Outside hand got him in trouble late. Sustaining movement in the run game was a struggle early. Started to figure out later in the game. Had a… pic.twitter.com/ZXsRp7HnKI — Geoff Schwartz (@geoffschwartz) August 14, 2026 “Pass pro looked clean. Moved feet well. Good strikes. Mixed up pass sets which I loved. Outside hand got him in trouble late,” Schwartz tweeted. “Sustaining movement in the run game was a struggle early. Started to figure out later in the game. Had a nice finish in the last clip. The thing I take away most is that he looked like he belonged. Sharp mentally as well. Handled some twists and movement well.” Long-time NFL guard Brian Baldinger also pitched in, and he uttered the same phrase that Schwartz did “looked like he belonged.” . @Lions @BlakeMillerOT played the entire first half…Looked like he belongs …Working v @aidanhutch97 everyday can speed up the learning phase… #onepride #BaldysBreakdowns pic.twitter.com/tyoweCY10h — Brian Baldinger (@BaldyNFL) August 14, 2026 “I thought it was a good debut for Blake Miller,” Baldinger concludes in his narration of the video. “Lot of football, played the entire first half. All you want to do is see improvement every day from him.” What I like about Baldinger’s breakdown is he doesn’t shy away from some of Miller’s less successful snaps. On one play, his initial set is good, but Miller allows a pressure to Bengals 2023 first-round pick Myles Murphy. But Miller wasn’t the only important offensive lineman on the field for the Lions against the Bengals. With Cade Mays’ broken wrist, suddenly reserve center Seth McLaughlin could be a critical player for the team, as he battles Juice Scruggs for the starting job. With Scruggs sidelined last week, McLaughlin got the start at center, logging his first NFL reps since his two rookie preseason performances last year. Offensive line analyst Brandon Thorn came away very impressed with McLaughlin’s game against the Bengals, and put together a string of his six best clips from the game. Seth McLaughlin has a big opportunity at center in Detroit. I was very high on him as a prospect relative to him going undrafted. He can play and I think had a promising first outing vs Cinci last night. Crafty, alert and tough. pic.twitter.com/1ZXpnoqev8 — Brandon Thorn (@BrandonThornNFL) August 14, 2026 Thorn wasn’t the only one who was impressed. Lions coach Dan Campbell offered significant praise for McLaughlin after the game. “He’s quick. He’s super sharp and he’s quick and he’s really good at the second level,” Campbell said. “And then pass game is the anchor. He’s just got to bend. And he’s got to do—in a lot of cases, he’s got to do double what somebody else does that has more stature, size or stature to him. That’s the hand he’s dealt. I thought he did that the other night. I did think he anchored better. I thought he strained. I though he tried to do all the little things and that’s a credit to him. So, I certainly was not disappointed with him the other day.” It’s just one game for each player, but I think it’s safe to say both had encouraging Lions debuts.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Detroit Lions roster bubble watch: Big questions at QB, WR
summary: The Detroit Lions have some big roster decisions to make in the upcoming weeks. Roster cutdown day is less than two weeks away, and time is running out to evaluate their players. On offense, Detroit has a conundrum at quarterback after Teddy Bridgewater’s retirement. But it’s a good conundrum, because both Luke Altmyer and Josh […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - AUGUST 13: Detroit Lions wide receiver Tay Martin (17) catches a pass during the game between the Detroit Lions and the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Cincinnati, OH. (Photo by Ian Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Detroit Lions have some big roster decisions to make in the upcoming weeks. Roster cutdown day is less than two weeks away, and time is running out to evaluate their players. On offense, Detroit has a conundrum at quarterback after Teddy Bridgewater’s retirement. But it’s a good conundrum, because both Luke Altmyer and Josh Dobbs were able to move the ball pretty well in the preseason opener. They apparently have a good problem at wide receiver, too. While there haven’t been any clear standouts beyond the top four players at that position, coach Dan Campbell believes that’s the deepest receiver group he’s ever been around in Detroit. “That receiver room, this is the best receiver room we’ve had since I’ve been here in camp, top to bottom,” Campbell said. “I mean, those guys are gifted. It’s a really good crew, man. And they’re all pretty tough, they’re all a little bit different the way they’re built. And every one of those guys has flashed on one day or another, has done something pretty damn good. So man, honestly, this thing’s up for grabs.” Let’s dive into each of those position battles on offense, as our staff makes their updated 2026 Detroit Lions roster bubble predictions: View Link Quarterback: Assumed in: Jared Goff Josh Dobbs: 9 “IN votes (no change) Luke Altmyer: 3 votes ( down 1 ) The backup quarterback job is heating up, but our staff still believes the Lions will go with the vetrean option. Altmyer had a strong preseason opener, but so did Dobbs—and Detroit opted to get him some time with the starters despite only joining the team a few days earlier. I’m a bit surprised that only one staffer opted to keep both quarterbacks, but I know there are some other positions that may warrant that roster spot over a QB3. Running back: Assumed in: Jahmyr Gibbs, Isiah Pacheco Sione Vaki: 11 votes (no change) Jacob Saylors: 11 votes ( up 2 ) Jabari Small: 0 votes Last week, we downgraded Vaki to the roster bubble because of his injury, but now that he has returned, he’s basically a lock. Coach Dan Campbell essentially referred to him as RB3 when talking about how Saylors and Smalls were fighting for that fourth spot. Saylors takes a jump in our votes after a strong preseason outing, while Small sat for injury. However, things could swap in a hurry now, because Small is back on the field, while Saylors is a nursing an ankle injury. Remember, Campbell called this RB4 battle neck-and-neck last week. “I feel like those two guys are just jockeying with each other right now. One guy’s a little bit ahead. The next day, the other guy’s a little bit ahead.” Wide receiver: Assumed in: Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams, Isaac TeSlaa, Greg Dortch Cedrick Wilson Jr.: 8 “IN” votes (up 1) New to bubble watch: Tay Martin: 4 votes Dominic Lovett: 3 votes (down 3) Tom Kennedy: 0 vote (no change) Tay Martin got an unprompted shout out by Dan Campbell, praising the former UFL receiver’s special teams skills. Since then, he’s been repping high on both special teams and offense. On Sunday, with Jameson Williams sidelined, Martin got some work with the first-team offense, suggesting he has truly climbed the depth chart. Three staffers have picked him as the team’s WR5, while another has Detroit keeping both Martin and Wilson. Most of Martin’s votes come at the expense of Lovett, who only caught three of his eight targets on Thursday night, had a couple of drops, and muffed a punt. He’s still flashing his separation skills and special teams potential, but there’s been too much bad with the good. Tight end: Assumed in: Sam LaPorta, Brock Wright OFF BUBBLE WATCH: Miles Kitselman (IR), Anthony Firkser (IR) Tyler Conklin: 11 “IN” votes (no change) Jackson Meeks: 2 votes (down 3) Thomas Gordon: 0 votes (no change) Meeks has had a bit of a quiet week, and as a result, our staffers are becoming less and less convinced Detroit will keep a fourth tight end. Personally speaking, Meeks was quite literally my last player out. I ultimately chose to keep an extra corner over Meeks, but it is not an easy decision right now. It’s entirely possible, though, Meeks could clear waivers (as he did last year) and come back on the practice squad. Offensive tackle: Assumed in: Penei Sewell, Blake Miller, Larry Borom Colby Sorsdal: 0 votes (no change) Devin Cochran: 0 votes (no change) Nothing changing here. Sorsdal continues to mostly rep with the third team, while Cochran has only recently been making his way back from injury. Interior offensive line: Assumed in: Tate Ratledge, Christian Mahogany, Miles Frazier NEW — Assumed on IR: Cade Mays Ben Bartch: 11 votes (no change) Juice Scruggs: 11 votes (up 0) Seth McLaughlin: 11 votes (up 11) Michael Niese: 0 votes Pretty simple adjustment here. With Cade Mays likely to start the season on injured reserve, all of his votes went straight to Seth McLaughlin, who now projects to be the team’s backup center behind Juice Scruggs. Of course, things could shift a bit depending on how the starting center job plays out. While Scruggs is the heavy favorite to win the job, the Lions appear to also be toying with the idea of playing Ratledge at center. If he were to somehow win the job, it would lessen the need for a third center behind Scruggs and jeopardize McLaughlin’s position. If the Lions are thinking about keeping only eight offensive linemen, that would be the route to take. For now, the entire staff has them keeping the exact same nine: Sewell, Miller, Borom, Ratledge, Mahogany, Frazier, Bartch, Scruggs, McLaughlin. One more thing to keep in mind: while he’s still very young and capable of playing multiple spots, Miles Frazier had a very tough preseason debut. If he struggles again in Saturday’s game against the Commanders, he could fall down to the bubble.

title: 2026 Detroit Lions 53-man roster prediction: Post-preseason Week 1
summary: The Detroit Lions walked away from their preseason game against the Cincinnati Bengals with a loss. Despite falling to 0-1 in the never-important preseason standings, it was a learning experience for all involved. Players got their first live reps of the 2026 season, coaches gained insight on their roster, fans got a look at new […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 28: Trevor Nowaske #53 of the Detroit Lions plays against the Cleveland Browns at Ford Field on September 28, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions walked away from their preseason game against the Cincinnati Bengals with a loss. Despite falling to 0-1 in the never-important preseason standings, it was a learning experience for all involved. Players got their first live reps of the 2026 season, coaches gained insight on their roster, fans got a look at new players, and media personnel learned how to pronounce difficult names like Amen Ogbongbemiga—preseason always matters. With one preseason game in the bag and two more still to come, has the Lions roster gained some clarity? Here is my projected 53-man roster, with plenty of difficult ins and outs to consider. Quarterbacks (2) QB Jared Goff QB Luke Altmyer QB Joshua Dobbs Right off the bat, we have a difficult choice. Do the Lions keep the more experienced and reliable Dobbs, do they keep the undrafted rookie who has shown promise thus far, or do they keep both? Initially, my choice was to keep three quarterbacks, but it led to a numbers crunch elsewhere on the roster. However, Dobbs has the benefit of not being subject to waivers due to his accrued seasons, and that led to some roster gymnastics. If the Lions cut Dobbs, I think the Lions could get the best of both worlds: keep Altmyer on the 53 and off waivers while also re-signing Dobbs to the practice squad and elevating him to the game-day roster for the first two weeks. By Week 3, perhaps the team will have more confidence in Altmyer as QB2 or an injury on the roster will open up a spot for Dobbs. This choice merely kicks the can down the road, but I see no harm in trying to keep both backups in the organization. Running backs (4) RB Jahmyr Gibbs RB Isiah Pacheco RB Sione Vaki RB Jacob Saylors RB Raheem Blackshear RB Jabari Small RB Trayveon Williams Personally, I think this room has been all but settled. Vaki has had a difficult start to training camp, but his value on special teams is unquestioned in the eyes of the coaching staff. Elsewhere, Saylors has taken a massive leap in the RB4 battle ahead of his contemporaries, and his contributions on special teams make keeping a fourth running back palatable—in fact, you could make an argument that Saylors is ahead of Vaki on offense. Wide receivers (5) WR Amon-Ra St. Brown WR Jameson Williams WR Isaac TeSlaa WR Greg Dortch WR Cedrick Wilson Jr. WR Tarik Black WR Malik Cunningham WR Lucky Jackson WR Tom Kennedy WR Dominic Lovett WR Tay Martin IR (season-ending): Kendrick Law Despite a slow start to training camp and a poor preseason showing against the Bengals, TeSlaa is still safely on this roster. As is Dortch, who looks like the team’s top returner option. That leaves one or two spots for reserves, and I currently have just Wilson taking that spot. I like Lovett’s ability to get open, but until he can corral the ball consistently, I can’t justify keeping him. Players like Black, Kennedy, and Martin are also in the hunt—all it could take is one big performance to reshuffle this depth chart. Tight ends (3) TE Sam LaPorta TE Brock Wright TE Tyler Conklin TE Thomas Gordon TE Zach Horton TE Jackson Meeks IR (season-ending): Anthony Firkser, Miles Kitselman I think that the top three are obvious locks, so the real debate is whether you keep a fourth tight end. Meeks is the frontrunner right now and him seeing action early in the preseason game shows that the coaching staff likes him ahead of his competition. I have him on the outs since I wanted to allocate that roster spot elsewhere, but he has the talent to strengthen his case in the coming weeks. Offensive linemen (9) LT Penei Sewell LG Christian Mahogany RG Tate Ratledge RT Blake Miller IOL Juice Scruggs OT Larry Borom OG Ben Bartch OG/OT Miles Frazier OC Seth McLaughlin OT Devin Cochran OG/OT Mason Miller IOL Michael Niese O G Melvin Priestly OT/OG Colby Sorsdal Assumed IR (not season-ending): Cade Mays Assumed NFI: Giovanni Manu The biggest question right now is the status of Mays and his wrist injury. As he is expected to miss a few months recovering, I think a stint on the Injured Reserve makes sense, ruling him out for at least four games. That leaves an opening at starting center, which will likely be filled by Scruggs ( although Ratledge getting first-team snaps in practice is an interesting wrinkle to watch for). Additionally, I think there is now an opening for a backup center behind Scruggs and McLaughlin’s encouraging preseason performance gives him an edge. Of the remaining reserves, the only question mark was Bartch due to his injury absence, but with his return to practice recently, I expect him to solidify his roster spot before long. Defensive tackles (6) DT Alim McNeill DT Tyleik Williams DL Levi Onwuzurike DL Tyler Lacy DT Skyler Gill-Howard DT Chris Smith DT Myles Adams DL Ben Stille DL Tyre West DT Mekhi Wingo IR (season-ending): Aidan Keanaaina I think the top five in this group are fairly obvious, although there is a non-zero chance that Onwuzurike could find himself on the roster bubble in the next few weeks if his game does not pick up soon. I have had Smith as in since the release of Jay Tufele, and he looks like the best nose tackle option behind McNeill and Williams. Wingo and West have disappointed thus far. Edge defenders (4) EDGE Aidan Hutchinson EDGE DJ Wonnum EDGE Derrick Moore EDGE Ahmed Hassanein EDGE Anthony Lucas EDGE Eric O’Neill EDGE Payton Turner Aside from Turner, the reserves in this group have impressed, but I only have room for one of them. Hassanein is teetering on the edge of being a lock, but I am not ready to solidify his roster spot yet. At least one of Lucas or O’Neill should be practice squad candidates. Turner, meanwhile, slides further and further behind as he continues to battle injury—the Marcus Davenport comparisons are not easing up. Linebackers (6) LB Jack Campbell LB Derrick Barnes LB Malcolm Rodriguez LB Trevor Nowaske LB Damone Clark LB Devin White LB Joe Bachie LB Erick Hunter LB Amen Ogbongbemiga LB Troy Reeder Assumed IR (not season-ending): Jimmy Rolder The health of Rolder is another significant question mark that could reshuffle this group. As a rookie that would be largely limited to special teams, I do not think they need to rush him back and can afford to stash him on IR to start the year. His injury prompted the Lions to sign White, and the veteran has thus far impressed—he may even jump Clark and Rodriguez on the depth chart and become the Lions’ LB3 or 4. I still believe that Nowaske (who donned the green dot against the Bengals) and Clark are good bets to make the roster thanks to their roles on special teams. Bachie and Ogbongbemiga have had positive moments, but they are on the outside looking in. Cornerbacks (7) CB D.J. Reed CB Rock Ya-Sin CB Roger McCreary CB Ennis Rakestraw CB Keith Abney CB Khalil Dorsey CB Nick Whiteside CB Ekow Boye-Doe CB Ryan “Bump” Cooper I went back and forth on this group for awhile, but I came to the conclusion that keeping seven cornerbacks makes sense. Whiteside has been the star of camp so far, and I cannot justify cutting him at this point. Elsewhere, Abney and McCreary had a great game against Cincinnati and look capable of playing inside or outside. Dorsey has quietly been playing well on defense, and his elite special teams ability should make him a safe roster choice. That leaves Rakestraw as the biggest question mark. He had a poor outing in preseason, not only in terms of coverage lapses but also because he suffered another injury. Sure, the injury was not severe (he returned to practice over the weekend), but for a player with limited tape, he needs to make the most of his live reps. The truth is that if he was not a second-round pick, I would have him as out. I don’t think the Lions are ready to give up on him yet, but he needs to justify…

title: Discussion: Which Detroit Lions should NOT play in the preseason?
summary: The Detroit Lions’ preparation for their second preseason game continues on Monday with their first night practice of training camp. That’s not the only thing that will be different this week. At least according to coach Dan Campbell’s comments earlier last week, the Lions will play their starters against the Washington Commanders on Saturday, the […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - AUGUST 20: Aidan Hutchinson #97 of the Detroit Lions walks off the field after the preseason game against the Indianapolis Colts at Lucas Oil Stadium on August 20, 2022 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions’ preparation for their second preseason game continues on Monday with their first night practice of training camp. That’s not the only thing that will be different this week. At least according to coach Dan Campbell’s comments earlier last week, the Lions will play their starters against the Washington Commanders on Saturday, the first time in several years under Campbell that they’ve decided to do so. “I think more of mine are the questions will be coming next week, when we start getting into the Washington week, because that was kind of where I always targeted like, alright, this may be where we need to play our guys,” Campbell said. “That’ll be the first one is kind of where I was thinking.” Jared Goff and Amon-Ra St. Brown haven’t played in the preseason since 2022. Jahmyr Gibbs has a total of 18 career preseason snaps since entering the league in 2023. Aidan Hutchinson has never played a single down of preseason football. So today’s Question of the Day is: Which Lions players should not play in the preseason? My answer: Well, if you need another reminder as to the risks of playing important players in the preseason, the Arizona Cardinals found out the hard way this weekend. First-round pick Jeremiyah Love reportedly suffered a high-ankle sprain, and now he could miss the start of the season. Personally, I would rather my team play it safe. I know the Lions haven’t traditionally played their best football early in the season and some believe shaking off rust in the preseason could help. But I find it hard to believe it makes a noticeable difference considering all of the work they get in training camp. That said, the Lions are running out of time to figure out key positions on the team—particularly on the offensive line and the secondary. They haven’t decided on the starting five on the offensive line, and positions like safety and nickel cornerback appear still in play. Because those positions also require a ton of chemistry, I am fully in favor of playing all of the projected starters on the offensive line and in the secondary. But do I need to see Jahmyr Gibbs or Jared Goff out there? No. Do I need to see St. Brown or Jamo or Jack Campbell or Aidan Hutchinson? No, I do not. I think you could make a strong argument for just about everyone else, though. Which Lions players do you think can skip out on this preseason? Share your thoughts in the comment section below.

It was a tumultuous spring for Trey Smack, and the Green Bay Packers’ rookie kicker had his share of issues early in training camp as well. The 6th-round pick out of Florida was inconsistent in practice for some time this year, and he has had to deal with adjusting to a new long snapper over the past few weeks with Cal Adomitis filling in for the injured Matt Orzech. Last Thursday, however, Smack showed why the Packers traded up for him in April. In his preseason debut, he hit all four of his field goal attempts at Pittsburgh’s Acrisure Stadium, including a pair from 58 yards out, one each in opposite directions. It was just the performance the Packers’ front office and coaching staff hoped to see from him, and it eased the minds of many Packers fans alike. Anders Carlson, Brayden Narveson, Brandon McManus, and Lucas Havrisik have all attempted kicks for the team over the past three years, with varying levels of inconsistency. By drafting Smack cutting McManus shortly thereafter, and releasing Havrisik early in training camp, the team has pushed all of its chips into the table for the youngster. Keisean Nixon, meanwhile, seems unhappy about his situation on the depth chart. That’s how it sounds, at least, but his complaints seem odd given that he has only rotated out of the starting lineup a handful of times in practice. Maybe the team needs to just give him a little bit more clarity with why he’s rotating out here and there; or maybe it’s just Keisean being Keisean and finding a way to motivate himself through perceived disrespect. Finally, Sunday’s practice was a big one for several young members of the secondary, as the unit picked up multiple interceptions against the first- and second-string offenses. We look at all of that and more in today’s curds. 5 things learned at Packers training camp – Aug. 16 | Packers.com There were a lot of interceptions on Sunday, from Kitan Oladapo picking off Jordan Love from the slot to Brandon Cisse getting Love and Jaylin Simpson nabbing a throw from Tyrod Taylor later on. title: Value of Things: What to expect from Brett Rypien
summary: For fans of a certain age, it becomes surreal to see sons of former legends currently playing. Brett Rypien is of course the son of former Redskins great Mark Rypien. Of course, when I say great it probably hyperbole. He led the Redskins to a Super Bowl, so I guess that makes him great. Is […]
full_text: For fans of a certain age, it becomes surreal to see sons of former legends currently playing. Brett Rypien is of course the son of former Redskins great Mark Rypien. Of course, when I say great it probably hyperbole. He led the Redskins to a Super Bowl, so I guess that makes him great. Is his son a chip off the old block or is he found lacking? The first thing we must do is adjust our expectations. We are looking for a third string quarterback. Tom Brady is not walking through that door. So, we are looking at Rypien as compared to Graham Mertz. The bad news is that Mertz never played a down in an actual game, so there is nothing to compare it to. However, we can compare Rypien with Davis Mills. In order to do this, we are condensing their performance to a per game basis. I am not simply looking at games played because backups often come into games late, so those results would be skewed. We are attempting to get as close as we can to 30 attempts per game so we can standardize the performance. It’s not perfect, but we can certainly get a handle on what we are looking at. Com ATT PCT YDS TD/INT Rating Davis Mills 18.5 29.9 61.8 191.4 1.1/0.7 82.5 Brett Rypien 19.6 33.6 58.3 190.0 0.8/1.8 59.9 There is a lot of secret sauce that goes into quarterback rating. These numbers look awfully similar for that much of a gap in rating. Mills takes better care of the football and is slightly more prolific in terms of touchdowns. However, these are two fairly similar quarterbacks. These numbers show that Mills should be the backup and Rypien’s presence is not really going to impact that. However, the source of our comparison is Mertz. Will Rypien be as good if not better than Mertz? That is a loaded question. In terms of who we would want out there in a game in 2026, Rypien is probably the answer every day and twice on Sunday. In terms of who will have the better career it might very well be Mertz. He has the higher ceiling although he will be returning from his second torn ACL. Below are the numbers for Mertz in the preseason for 2025 and 2026. Com ATT PCT YDS TD/INT 2025 23 32 71.9 174 1/3 2026 4 7 57.1 23 0/0 Total 27 39 69.1 197 1/3 These numbers are not radically different than what Mills and Rypien were putting up on a per game basis. Of course, we have the normal caveats of playing against vanilla defenses with second or third string talent out there on both sides of the ball. Suffice it to say, it looks like the Texans have replaced their third string quarterback with a comparable quarterback. The final question is more of a philosophical one. What should teams do with that third quarterback slot? Do you want another steady hand that can backup the backup? Do you want a developmental guy that could convert raw skills into something more tangible down the road? Do you want an athletic quarterback that could come on the field on certain gadget plays or certain formation packages that could take advantage of a specific skillset? Every team handles it differently.

title: BREAKING: Colts reportedly sign former Pro Bowl veteran wideout Keenan Allen
summary: With lead wideout Alec Pierce still recovering from off-season ankle surgery, the Indianapolis Colts wide receiver room was beginning to feel concerning. A single injury to Josh Downs (who recently left practice with what was described as an “upper body injury”) could have been catastrophic to the offense’s chance to repeat the success it had […]
full_text: Jul 26, 2023; Costa Mesa, CA, USA; Los Angeles Chargers receiver Keenan Allen (13) catches the ball during training camp at Jack Hammett Sports Complex. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-USA TODAY Sports | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con With lead wideout Alec Pierce still recovering from off-season ankle surgery, the Indianapolis Colts wide receiver room was beginning to feel concerning. A single injury to Josh Downs (who recently left practice with what was described as an “upper body injury”) could have been catastrophic to the offense’s chance to repeat the success it had during the first half of 2025. Enter Keenan Allen. BREAKING: The #Colts are signing 6x Pro Bowl WR Keenan Allen to a 1-year deal worth up to $8.32M, multiple sources tell me. A big-time weapon for Daniel Jones, as Allen reunites with HC Shane Steichen from their days together with the Chargers in a deal done by @ZekeSandhu of… pic.twitter.com/wiBZe3wjSf — Jordan Schultz (@Schultz_Report) August 18, 2026 In the weeks leading up to training camp and the preseason, many speculated that Indy could be interested in Allen in the days and weeks leading up to the start of the season. It made sense. He needed a team. The Colts needed a receiver. Indy has an offensive play caller very familiar with the veteran receiver and more importantly, Allen’s familiarity with Steichen’s offensive system. Specifically, coaching Allen, Steichen served as an offensive assistant for the Chargers from 2014-20, including being their offensive coordinator during his final season in Los Angeles. Most of the time roster moves this obvious don’t happen for one reason or another, but this ended up being the rare NFL scenario of what seemed like such an obvious solution, actually happening. Time will tell if this signing will move any needles for an Indy offense that will likely lean hard on second year tight end Tyler Warren, and it’s ground game headed up by Jonathan Taylor, as always. But on paper signing a former six time Pro Bowler who caught 81 passes a season ago, this move though not flashy, could end up being just what the offense needs to continue to grow, evolve and produce the kinds of results everyone in the Colts’ building is hoping for and expecting. I have been told that this deal has taken quite a bit of time to hammer out, and it isn’t something the Colts recently decided to do. If that’s true (and I have no reason to believe it isn’t), there’s no reason to panic over Alec Pierce’s ankle or Josh Downs’ recent practice injury. At least not yet. Stay tuned.

title: Colts indicate their current intentions to keep QB Anthony Richardson Sr.
summary: According to their assistant general manager Ed Dodds, the Indianapolis Colts currently plan on keeping backup quarterback Anthony Richardson Sr., as they intend on keeping three quarterbacks and aren’t wanting to detract from their current team (via The Athletic’s James Boyd). Now, if the Colts had gotten meaningful trade value back in a swap for […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 13: Anthony Richardson Sr. #5 of the Indianapolis Colts looks on in the first quarter against the New England Patriots at Gillette Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Jaiden Tripi/Getty Images) | Getty Images According to their assistant general manager Ed Dodds, the Indianapolis Colts currently plan on keeping backup quarterback Anthony Richardson Sr., as they intend on keeping three quarterbacks and aren’t wanting to detract from their current team (via The Athletic’s James Boyd). Now, if the Colts had gotten meaningful trade value back in a swap for Richardson Sr., who requested a trade earlier this offseason, then he would realistically be elsewhere right now to that generous suitor. That being said, such a trade doesn’t appear to have materialized, and while a significant quarterback injury could certainly happen, most teams already have their backup quarterback plans in place entering the second week of preseason. Colts longtime general manager Chris Ballard indicated earlier this offseason that the Colts weren’t simply going to give away Richardson Sr., still believing he has value and upside. To be fair too, their starting quarterback, Daniel Jones, is coming off a late season torn Achilles and hasn’t exactly been an ‘NFL ironman’ himself, even dating back to his days as a former franchise quarterback hopeful with the New York Giants. While he clearly started out rusty, Richardson Sr. actually progressed nicely in his 2026 preseason debut, completing 11 of 14 pass attempts for 145 passing yards and an interception (*which should’ve been caught) to go along with his 53 total rushing yards and rushing touchdown on 6 carries against the New England Patriots. It was that dynamic rushing ability which doesn’t play out as well in Colts camp, but was on full display in this past Thursday night’s exhibition game—with the ability to make plays outside the pocket and downfield. In contrast, 2nd-year quarterback Riley Leonard, who is Richardson’s competition for the Colts QB2 job behind Jones, had a fairly rough preseason showing in relief during the second half—and with only 1 career start under his belt, could arguably use a bit more seasoning before being anointed Indy’s primary backup quarterback. Richardson is entering the last year of his rookie contract and clearly is looking for a fresh start elsewhere, but if the Colts can’t get a worthwhile trade return, it makes sense to keep him around for 2026 as their QB2. Given what happened with Jones late last season, you never know when Richardson Sr.‘s next opportunity could arise and who knows, perhaps there’s still time to rewrite how his chapter ultimately ends in Indianapolis.

title: Colts work out experienced veteran offensive guard, among other offensive linemen
summary: According to the NFL transaction wire, the Indianapolis Colts worked out former Arizona Cardinals and New York Giants offensive guard Will Hernandez, along with offensive tackles Trey Wedig and D’Ante Smith. Originally a 2018 2nd round pick of the Giants, the 30-year-old veteran offensive guard is likely most well known by Colts fans as being […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 08: Will Hernandez #76 of the Arizona Cardinals lines up during the first quarter against the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium on September 08, 2024 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images According to the NFL transaction wire, the Indianapolis Colts worked out former Arizona Cardinals and New York Giants offensive guard Will Hernandez, along with offensive tackles Trey Wedig and D’Ante Smith. Originally a 2018 2nd round pick of the Giants, the 30-year-old veteran offensive guard is likely most well known by Colts fans as being the 2nd best offensive guard prospect in the same prior draft class as perennial Indianapolis All-Pro left guard Quenton Nelson. Of course, the 8-year veteran Hernandez has gone on to appear in 104 career games (98 starts). While he doesn’t have the same league-wide accolades as Nelson, he’s carved out a fairly lengthy starting NFL career himself. However, he started in 7 games last year, earning a +45.3 overall grade, which ranked just 77th among 81 qualifying guards. He started just 5 games a year prior in 2024, having suffered a season-ending knee injury. While Colts rookie 4th round pick Jalen Farmer has looked pretty good so far throughout training camp and in his preseason debut, it couldn’t hurt to add a backup offensive guard with a wealth of experience into the mix. With Danny Pinter’s departure, Colts 3rd-year guard Dalton Tucker is now transitioning to backup center, which means Indianapolis could use another capable interior offensive lineman for depth. Hernandez had a rough season last year, but one should still look at his complete body of work—as he’s only 30-years-old and could be a ‘plug-and-play’ interior offensive lineman off the bench if called upon. Meanwhile, Hedwig is a 6,7”, 313 pound offenive tackle who the Horseshoe Faithful may already know from his time with the Indiana Hoosiers (2024). Signed as an undrafted rookie free agent by the Los Angeles Rams in 2025, he’s also spent time with the Arizona Cardinals organization and most recently, the UFL’s DC Defenders. Lastly, D’Ante Smith is a 6,5”, 309 pound offensive tackle, who was initially a 2021 4th round pick of the Cincinnati Bengals, where he played from 2021-24, appearing in 3 career games (1 start).
author: Luke Schultheis

title: Chiefs training camp notebook Day 15: Offense is honing in on details
summary: Monday was the 15th full-team practice of Kansas City Chiefs training camp, a full-padded session that followed Saturday’s preseason opener, which ended in a 20-12 defeat to the Los Angeles Rams. An injury-status update from head coach Andy Reid can be found here. After the game, Reid’s biggest note of criticism for his team centered […]
full_text: Kansas City Chiefs head coach Andy Reid, left, speaks with wide receiver Xavier Worthy (1) during practice at training camp on Friday, July 31, 2026, in St. Joseph. (Emily Curiel/Kansas City Star/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) Monday was the 15th full-team practice of Kansas City Chiefs training camp, a full-padded session that followed Saturday’s preseason opener, which ended in a 20-12 defeat to the Los Angeles Rams . An injury-status update from head coach Andy Reid can be found here . After the game, Reid’s biggest note of criticism for his team centered around the 12 penalties called on Kansas City. He elaborated on that issue — which was almost entirely on the offense — after Monday’s practice at training camp in St. Joe. “Obviously, the five holding calls and the five illegal-procedure penalties: you can’t have those,” Reid said. “You have to be more disciplined than that, so we go back and keep stressing that.” “On the offensive line, we’re overshooting things a little bit, and we have to make sure we cover up bodies on that in the run game,” Reid explained about the penalties. “In the pass game, you have to let go; there’s a time and place where you have to let go. “It’s not an effort thing; it’s putting yourself in the right position,” Reid continued. “Disciplining it, and you do the same thing in practice; you work on that.” With those coaching points, it isn’t surprising that the Chiefs held another high-intensity practice on the grass fields at Missouri Western State University to start this week. EB just told someone to “shut the [expletive] up” after a play in 7 on 7 lol — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) August 17, 2026 Offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy was hard on the starting offense, including a pointed effort to make wide receiver Rashee Rice finish through a play after the catch. The fourth-year wideout was jogging back to the huddle before Bieniemy’s remarks had him turning back around and running downfield again. Earlier in the practice, when the quarterbacks and receivers were running routes on air on the far field, first-year wide receivers coach Chad O’Shea could be heard imploring his players. “Details, guys! Details,” O’Shea said loudly before instructing a receiver to run his route again. At the podium, Reid was asked about what he has seen from new assistant coaches like O’Shea or running backs coach DeMarco Murray. “I like the detail that they’re bringing to the group there,” Reid responded. “They’re staying on the guys… they’ve got some young guys that they’re dealing with, and new guys… there’s a lot of teaching going on, and they’re doing a good job of doing the teaching.” Offensive lineup notes Jaylon Moore gets a look at right guard Speaking of details, there are a lot of them that go into each position along the offensive line. Chiefs offensive line coach Andy Heck has always made an effort to cross-train Kansas City’s young players in order to maximize their talent, and that has been the case with rookie Kahlil Benson this camp. He has played both guard and tackle on the right side, and now veteran Jaylon Moore is working into that same kind of versatile role as the team continues on without starting right guard Trey Smith (Hip). Reid provided (a little) more clarity on how the team has been handling the competition at right tackle, now less than a month until Week 1. “Moore has been doing a great job in there for us, but with that, Benson doesn’t get any reps at it,” Reid explained. “We want him to go against the better players and have a chance to continue to grow there. So we just flopped them over and let Moore get some reps at guard, and Benson get some reps at the tackle spot.” “Benson held his own at the guard spot in the game,” Reid elaborated. “They need to be able to play both as we go through this thing. It’s good experience, but it’s not one over the other. Moore has put together a lot of good days here and played [well] the other night.” Emmett Johnson takes the second reps at running back After one snap of running back Kenneth Walker in Saturday’s preseason game, second-year back Brashard Smith came in and made a nice play on a screen pass that wasn’t well-blocked. It was a flash of Smith’s playmaking, but rookie running back Emmett Johnson looked much more comfortable and more effective on traditional handoffs. To me, it wasn’t surprising that Johnson has supplanted Smith as the second back in drills at practice. Still, Johnson has details to hone if he wants to build on this momentum. “He ran hard, some of his footwork… I’m not saying he went the wrong way,” Reid began. “But we tried to tie the footwork up for the back with the offensive line; you have to be able to set those guys up. There has to be a certain amount of patience, and your angle becomes important on that that you take to the line of scrimmage, so he could work on that.” “As far as the effort and the ability to make people miss, you got a pretty good idea of his vision,” Reid reflected. “All of those things were positives.” Other notes from practice Second-year defensive end Ashton Gillotte returned to fully participate in practice, picking up a unique role the Chiefs teased during the first portion of camp. In the starting base defense, Gillotte played the SAM linebacker role, the strong-side player who represents a fifth man on the line of scrimmage; he lined up next to down linemen George Karlaftis, Chris Jones, Khyiris Tonga and R Mason Thomas. Speaking of Thomas, it felt like he overtook the first-team snaps that fourth-year defensive end Felix Anudike-Uzomah was seeing prior to the first preseason game. During the walkthrough portions of early practice, Anudike-Uzomah was exclusively with the second-team unit on the other side of the field. Wide receiver Xavier Worthy participated in practice and made a big play in seven-on-seven, but he was not a full participant. In 11-on-11 periods, the starting receivers were Rashee Rice, Tyquan Thornton and rookie Cyrus Allen. Anecdotally, Allen has a stronger spot in the rotation than second-year wideout Jalen Royals does. The team will be back at practice in St. Joe on Tuesday morning, starting at 9:15 a.m.

title: Andy Reid provides injury update after Monday’s Chiefs camp practice
summary: After the Kansas City Chiefs’ first preseason game of the 2026 campaign, head coach Andy Reid had just one injury to report: offensive tackle Chu Godrick sprained his ankle. Back at training camp on Monday, Godrick didn’t participate in practice. A few of his teammates along the offensive line eventually came off the field too. […]
full_text: Kansas City Chiefs head coach Andy Reid observes players during practice at Chiefs training camp on Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026, in St. Joseph. (Emily Curiel/Kansas City Star/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) After the Kansas City Chiefs ’ first preseason game of the 2026 campaign, head coach Andy Reid had just one injury to report: offensive tackle Chu Godrick sprained his ankle. Back at training camp on Monday, Godrick didn’t participate in practice. A few of his teammates along the offensive line eventually came off the field too. Reid shared the injury rundown with local media after the first practice sessions of the week on the grass fields at Missouri Western State University in St. Joe. “Today, [Matt] Waletzko hurt his knee out here,” Reid shared. “Not sure how bad it is. We’ll just get it checked here.” “[Esa] Pole had some dehydration,” Reid added, tallying three reserve offensive linemen that were unavailable by the end of Monday’s practice. Starting left tackle Josh Simmons had to step in for the third team briefly due to the injuries. Right guard Trey Smith also continued to be held out of practice, working off to the side in the medical tent. It doesn’t sound like the team’s starting guard on the right side will be back on the practice field before the team leaves St. Joe after the final practice on Thursday. “Trey’s doing good,” Reid shared. “We’ll see; he’s getting close, so we’ll see where it goes here. I don’t know if you’ll see him this week, but he’s getting close.” While the offensive line works back to full health, there were two other players who left practice: rookie safety DeShon Singleton and veteran linebacker Jack Cochrane. “Singleton tweaked his hamstring a little bit,” Reid told the press. “Then Cochrane’s knee, but he finished practice there.” Rookie, No. 6 overall pick Mansoor Delane participated in a full-contact practice for the first time this preseason. He was the starting cornerback opposite Nohl Williams for the first-team defense throughout the day. “He did everything and was in all the drills,” Reid described Delane. “He looked good; it was good work for him.” Reid shared that the team’s doctors have examined Delane recently. There are positive indicators that Delane is ready to play at full speed. “It looks like he’s healing up pretty good, enough to where he can get out here and do some things,” Reid said. “Then we’ll just monitor and see how he does with the extended play. He hasn’t taken that many reps as what he did today, so we’ll just see how he does.” Other players who didn’t participate in Monday’s practice Wide receiver Jimmy Holiday Safety Chamarri Conner Cornerback Kader Kohou (Sore knee) Defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott (PUP) Cornerback L’Jarius Sneed (Knee management) Linebacker Drue Tranquill (Back spasms) Wide receiver Jeff Weimer

title: Chiefs Preseason Week 1 snap count analysis: Jaden Hicks gets extended time
summary: Welcome back to Arrowhead Pride’s weekly snap-count analysis! During the preseason, we will shorten the analysis as it is difficult to make definitive statements based on the raw snap-count data. Still, let’s see what we can figure out about the Kansas City Chiefs when taking a closer look at playing time during the 20-12 loss […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - AUGUST 15: Los Angeles Rams tight end Max Klare (86) reaches for a pass around Kansas City Chiefs safety Jaden Hicks (21) during the first halfon August 15th at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by William Purnell/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome back to Arrowhead Pride’s weekly snap-count analysis! During the preseason, we will shorten the analysis as it is difficult to make definitive statements based on the raw snap-count data. Still, let’s see what we can figure out about the Kansas City Chiefs when taking a closer look at playing time during the 20-12 loss at the hands of the Los Angeles Rams on Saturday. Starters (offensive): LT Josh Simmons, LG Kingsley Suamataia, C Creed Humphrey, RG Kahlil Benson, RT Jaylon Moore, QB Justin Fields, WR Tyquan Thornton, WR Jalen Royals, WR Cyrus Allen, RB Kenneth Walker, TE Noah Gray Starters (defensive): DE George Karlaftis, DT Chris Jones, DT Khyiris Toga, DE Felix Anudike-Uzomah, LB Nick Bolton, LB Jeffrey Bassa, S Christian Roland-Wallace, CB Nohl Williams, CB Melvin Smith, S Jaden Hicks, S Alohi Gilman Did not play: QB Patrick Mahomes. TE Travis Kelce, WR Rashee Rice (Knee), WR Jimmy Holiday, RG Trey Smith (Hip), S Chamarri Conner, LB Drue Tranquill (Back spasms), CB Mansoor Delane (Shoulder), CB L’Jarius Sneed (Knee), CB Kader Kohou (Sore Knee), DE Ashton Gillotte (Hamstring), DE Emmanuel Ogbah The big takeaway Third-year safety Jaden Hicks started the game on defense and all four phases of special teams: kickoff, kick return, punt and punt return. With injuries/DNPs to keep in mind, these are the Chiefs players who were on the field for the first snap of all four Special Teams phases (KO, KR, Punt, PR) S Jaden Hicks TE Jared Wiley LB Jeffrey Bassa LB Cole Christiansen — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) August 16, 2026 He played early and often, finishing the game with a team-leading 33 defensive snaps. The extended playing time was a welcome sight and likely warmly received by Hicks, who has seen little time with the starting defense in training camp, with starting safeties Chamarri Conner and Alohi Gilman taking almost every significant rep on the first team. The unfortunate injury to Conner last week gave Hicks a chance to play next to Gilman with the starting defense, but Hicks’ additional snaps with the reserve units were still significant; defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo needs to see as much as he can from Hicks before deciding to carve a role out for him in the starting defense. According to Pro Football Focus, Hicks played 16 snaps as a deep safety, 15 snaps in the box, and two aligned in the slot. He led the team with five solo tackles, two stops and a pass breakup. The Offensive takeaway Of the non-linemen, wide receiver Andrew Armstrong led all Chiefs players in offensive snaps with 41, tying quarterback Garrett Nussmeier. Armstrong also played five snaps on special teams. Armstrong made his presence felt on the field, whether the play call was a run or a pass. He started his time on the field with a nice catch and turned up the sideline; later, he appeared to have a step on a deep pass towards the back line of the end zone, but the pass from Nussmeier was too far. Wide Receiver LAUNCH of the DB!! Love these pic.twitter.com/2m4vdzKGCG — Mitchell Schwartz (@MitchSchwartz71) August 15, 2026 When he blocked, he didn’t waste the reps. He has made a strong impression in camp as a pass catcher, but Armstrong took advantage of his first chance at true live contact. The Defensive takeaway Fourth-year defensive end Felix Anudike-Uzomah played the fourth-most snaps (27) of all Chiefs players on defense. However, only 19 of those reps occurred with the former Kansas State Wildcat aligned on the edge. FAU aligned inside (B-gap) on 8 of his 27 plays Saturday per PFF No other Chiefs DE recorded an interior snap. Feels like he’s settling into a niche role in Spags’ NASCAR 3rd down packages — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) August 16, 2026 The other eight snaps were spent lined up further inside, in the B gap, according to PFF . That’s notable because no other defensive end aligned anywhere but over or outside the tackle. During training camp, Anudike-Uzomah has lined up inside for pass-rush looks, like the front for a six-defensive-back Dime look. He joins Chris Jones, George Karlaftis, and R Mason Thomas most of the time. With the signing of veteran defensive end Emmanuel Ogbah, there are signs pointing to Anudike-Uzomah settling into a niche role in the Chiefs’ third-down pass rush, being the next edge rusher shifting inside in Spagnuolo’s “NASCAR package.” Editor’s Note : Arrowhead Pride will present charts with updated snap-count data in this weekly post during the regular season.

title: Chiefs News: Garrett Nussmeier makes a good impression in NFL debut
summary: The latest The Kansas City Chiefs’ 2026 draft class was ready to play a football game donning the red and gold for the first time on Saturday, and many fans had their eyes glued to those specific newcomers. Rookie running back Emmett Johnson was a standout; wide receiver Cyrus Allen made a highlight-reel catch, and […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - AUGUST 15: Quarterback Garrett Nussmeier #14 of the Kansas City Chiefs throws a second quarter pass against the Los Angeles Rams at Arrowhead Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images The latest The Kansas City Chiefs ’ 2026 draft class was ready to play a football game donning the red and gold for the first time on Saturday, and many fans had their eyes glued to those specific newcomers. Rookie running back Emmett Johnson was a standout; wide receiver Cyrus Allen made a highlight-reel catch, and edge rusher R Mason Thomas did his best to show off his skill set. All that said, seventh-round pick Garrett Nussmeier’s confidence and poise may have popped off the screen the most once he took the reins from Justin Fields on the third drive of the game. Chiefs preseason opener yields promising performances from rookies, questions on offensive line | KCTV5 Third-string quarterback Garrett Nussmeier completed 13 of 19 passes for 98 yards. Head coach Andy Reid said the rookie handled the moment well. “For his first time out there rolling, I thought he handled it well, made some nice throws, had some long yardage situations and handled it well. And did a good job there,” Reid said. Veteran Justin Fields, competing with Nussmeier to serve as Patrick Mahomes’ backup, completed all four of his pass attempts for 41 yards. Why Chiefs rookies were the biggest story of preseason opener vs. the Rams | The Athletic Not only did Armstrong use his 6-foot-4 size to bring down a sideline catch early on, but he also went viral online afterward for his blocking, putting Rams defenders on their backsides twice on running plays. Armstrong said those knockdowns were a specialty of his in college at Arkansas. “I know coming in here, a lot of people are not expecting it,” Armstrong said in the locker room with a smile. “So that’s when you can get them.” Armstrong said he modeled his blocking after Dallas Cowboys wideout George Pickens, who has displayed similar bouts of aggressiveness. “I love to block. I love to do those things,” Armstrong said. “So if the coaches love that as well and I love to do that, I hope that would be a great asset to them.” How Chiefs DB Kaiir Elam hopes to avoid ‘bust’ label with a comeback in KC | The Kansas City Star Most NFL teams, especially the Chiefs, will sign a former first-round pick to a one-year “prove it” deal, like Elam did in April. At 25 years old, he’s looking to put his best foot forward as he works his way through training camp in just his fifth season. “Just giving the best version of myself,” Elam told The Star. “I feel like I haven’t really shown the best version of myself yet in this league. So just being the best version of myself with the opportunities that I do earn.” Elam has started only 19 of the 43 total games he’s appeared in over four years, tallying 114 tackles, eight passes defensed, and two interceptions (both in his rookie season). Elam also recorded two interceptions in five playoff appearances. Chiefs Rookie R Mason Thomas Flashes Glimpses of Potential in Preseason Opener | Sports Illustrated Standing at 6-foot-2, 241 pounds, most pre-draft scouts viewed Thomas as a player who would need to add more weight before becoming an every-down option. However, he made an impact in the run game, shedding blocks and forcing Rams tailbacks to avoid him at all costs. We even saw some examples of Thomas bull-rushing L.A.’s offensive linemen. He may be regarded as a speed rusher, but Thomas told reporters after the game that he’s no one-trick pony. “I don’t know why people regard me as a speed-rusher,” Thomas said. “I do bull. I did bull at college, too. I guess it’s my stature, my weight, they classify me as speed.” 5 takeaways from Kansas City Chiefs’ preseason opener against Los Angeles Rams | KSHB 41 5. Mixed results for rookie DL It’s no secret that Kansas City’s defensive line wasn’t good enough in 2025, so it also wasn’t a surprise to see the Chiefs invest two of their first three picks, No. 29 and 40 overall, in defensive linemen. Peter Woods has impressed in training camp with his work ethic and demeanor, but he is also battling an ankle injury. The rookie first-round defensive tackle from Clemson struggled to hold the line of scrimmage and didn’t record a stat in limited snaps. Chiefs-Rams: 9 things that stood out in Kansas City’s first preseason game | KMBC Here’s the encouraging counterpoint – the Chiefs got off the field on third down. Los Angeles converted only two third downs all game, a significant improvement in an area that caused Kansas City plenty of frustration last season. Third-down defense involves far more than the secondary. Pressure, coverage and tackling all have to work together. Around the NFL Retired Aaron Donald works out for Rams for second time | ESPN Donald’s “tryout” at the team’s Woodland Hills facility was listed Sunday on the NFL’s transaction report. It was his second time working out for the team this training camp. Coach Sean McVay said Donald’s decision will come on “his timeline.” “What I don’t want is to sit here and do is put a timeline on it, then something comes up where I have to push it back,” McVay said after the Rams’ preseason opener in Kansas City on Saturday night. Cowboys agree to terms with eight-time Pro Bowl pass rusher Von Miller | NFL.com Miller, who grew up in DeSoto, Texas, and played collegiately at Texas A&M, understandably waited until the dog days of summer were mostly over before joining a new squad, but he seemingly has plenty still left to give as a pass rusher. He’s the current active leader in career sacks with 138.5, having racked up nine last year to lead the Commanders despite starting only three of 17 games. That number was the most since a 9.5-sack effort combined between the Broncos and Rams in 2021, a year that divides Miller’s career quite cleanly. Arizona Cardinals rookie running back Jeremiyah Love dealing with a high ankle sprain | Revenge of The Birds Jeremiyah Love is dealing with a high ankle sprain after his 14 touch first half in the preseason win for the Arizona Cardinals over the Las Vegas Raiders. Love was ‘s final touch of the game was also the play where he was injured, and many in the non-Cardinals media world wondered aloud if it was bad. This is a tough one, and hopefully five weeks between the injury and game one will be more than enough for Love to rehab and get back, but a high ankle sprain is a typical three week injury, and can be a little bit of a pain to come back from. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride Chiefs rookie back Emmett Johnson ‘ran hard and aggressive’ “He did a nice job with it,” Reid told local media in his post-game press conference. “He ran hard and aggressive, had some yards after contact there, which is a big thing. He was one of the positives coming out of this, I thought he did a nice job.” Johnson displayed an aggressive and tough running style. He read blocks and hit the available holes hard, without hesitation. He was the main cog in the Chiefs’ offensive attack in the preseason opener. “He has a good feel,” Reid continued to praise the rookie’s first performance. “He’s patient, then when he hits it, he hits it hard. He has a toughness to him there. I know the offensive linemen appreciate that.” From The Feed Follow Arrowhead Pride on Social Media Facebook: Like our page Instagram: @ArrowheadPride X: Follow @ArrowheadPride AP Staff on X: See complete list 90.9 The Bridge on X: Follow @909thebridge

title: 5 Rams questions I have after first preseason game
summary: Saturday’s game between the Los Angeles Rams and the Kansas City Chiefs brought answers and left us with some significant questions. There remain two exhibition games to collect information ahead of the page turning to the regular season. If searching for answers to the leftover burning questions, these are the areas I would start: 1 […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - AUGUST 15: Head coach Sean McVay of the Los Angeles Rams reacts after a penalty call in the second quarter during an NFL preseason game against the Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images Saturday’s game between the Los Angeles Rams and the Kansas City Chiefs brought answers and left us with some significant questions. There remain two exhibition games to collect information ahead of the page turning to the regular season. If searching for answers to the leftover burning questions, these are the areas I would start: 1 – Why are Rams set in their ways at punt returner? Despite watching Xavier Smith quite literally fumble away the NFC Championship game last season, he returns as LA’s primary punt returner. The Rams had all offseason to either bring in competition or consider alternatives. Instead, they seem ready to run it back with Smith. But why? Smith brings little upside to the return role, even if he did break a longer return for one of the most important plays in Saturday’s game in KC. Can the Rams maximize a roster spot by identifying a player who can contribute more as a returner and elsewhere? I’d start with receiver Brennan Presley, who played well in the 2025 exhibition games and then led the Rams in receiving yards against the Chiefs. Presley has a similarly sized frame and close skillset to Smith. He seems to be a more productive receiver and the team risks nothing by experimenting with him as a punt returner. Presley already returned kicks in the preseason opener. Push his limits and see what he is capable of. I’d also suggest standout running back Dean Connors as an option. Connors has an uphill battle to make the roster but could usurp second-year back Jarquez Hunter. Why not see if his athleticism translates to the third phase? 2 – Can Stetson Bennett make a comeback in QB battle? The early indications from training camp suggested that Bennett was well ahead of rookie Ty Simpson. That momentum faded in the final days at Loyola Marymount and in the joint practice session against the Dallas Cowboys. Bennett did little to impress on Saturday, and drew the lowest Pro Football Focus (PFF) grade on offense . Was Bennett’s early camp success overstated? Is he simply in a lull right now? He’ll need to prove his struggles are only temporary—or he could find himself looking for work in a matter of weeks. 3 – Will Jarquez Hunter make the 53-man roster? Hunter and Connors are evidently the fastest running backs on the Rams’ roster. Hunter broke an outside run for 11 yards early and played sparingly. Veteran Ronnie Rivers sat out of the first preseason game, which could signal that he’s already made the team. It will be tough for the Rams to keep four running backs on the 53-man roster, especially to make room for Hunter who hasn’t shown much through two years. Connors arguably could be a more useful player given his skillset as a receiver, especially if he gets an opportunity as a returner. Connors should play much earlier in the remaining two games. Hunter may not be competing with Rivers but rather with the guy who was sixth on the depth chart a week ago. 4 – Was CJ Daniels’ training camp overhyped? One of the most praised players in the first days of training camp before the pads came on was rookie receiver CJ Daniels. Similar to Bennett, the positive reports surrounding Daniels faded once practices grew more physical. It’s relatively easy for receivers to become preseason stars. We’ve certainly seen such outcomes from less talented players over the years, and Puka Nacua immediately looked like a force during his rookie campaign. Daniels is probably safe to make the roster. If he wants to step foot on the field as a meaningful contributor, he needs to make splash plays. Should Daniels stay on his current path, he will remain entrenched behind Jordan Whittington and Konata Mumpfield on the depth chart. 5 – What more do we need to see from Ty Simpson? Simpson did not attempt a single throw over 20 yards or generate a big-time throw on Saturday. That is really the last box we need to check from a skillset perspective. The Rams must open the playbook and Simpson needs to make big plays without putting the ball in harm’s way. It’s no secret that Simpson doesn’t have Matthew Stafford’s arm talent. He still has plenty of juice for a player with a slight frame. His velocity in Kansas City looked good, even when he was throwing on the move. But if Simpson continues to live in the short to intermediate areas of the field, he will develop a reputation as a check down artist. First impressions matter at the quarterback position—just ask Jared Goff. The rookie needs to check this box sooner than later.
author: JB Scott

title: Myles Garrett, Puka Nacua absences will be prolonged

Although McVay stated last week that Nacua would return to practice, the head coach has now pushed his […]
full_text: LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA - JULY 27: Head coach Sean McVay of the Los Angeles Rams talks with Myles Garrett #95 during the Los Angeles Rams Training Camp at Loyola Marymount University on July 27, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Katelyn Mulcahy/Getty Images) | Getty Images Neither Myles Garrett nor Puka Nacua were supposed to be missing this many practices based on initial reports, but the Los Angeles Rams don’t expect to get either star player back this week, according to Sean McVay. Although McVay stated last week that Nacua would return to practice, the head coach has now pushed his return to next week. The same goes for Garrett, although McVay would only go as far to say “probably” for both players. The Rams have pushed all-in with their moves to acquire players like Garrett in an offseason trade, but so far his training camp has been more like “all out”. Takeaways from Sean McVay on Monday: 🔵 Puka Nacua (psoas) and Myles Garrett (knee): “Probably next week when we get those guys back.” 🔵 OL Keagen Trost (hamstring) and WR Mario Williams (hamstring) out for a “few weeks.” 🔵 Aaron Donald’s workout was “semantical,” per McVay. — Benjamin Royer (@thebenroyer) August 17, 2026 Garrett’s knee injury has caused him to miss the equivalent of two weeks of training camp. That’s about to go up to three weeks. Nacua’s hip injury (psoas) occurred during joint practice with the Dallas Cowboys last Tuesday . This sounds like more than a “hangnail”, as fans were hoping it would be when the injury was first reported. Being careful with players who are important for Week 1 is not surprising, but same as Matthew Stafford last year, the severity or timeline to return seems to get more significant by the day. And what happened to Stafford? He didn’t miss a single important snap. So the Rams may not have anything to worry about with regards to these absences. It’s worth keeping tabs on their progress however since they are so important, the team has invested so much, and the Rams are about to travel across the world for a football game.

title: Liam Coen regrets decision to leave Rams after 2022 season
summary: Liam Coen was on The Pivot Podcast when he spoke about one of his biggest coaching regrets, and it boiled down to Coen leaving the Los Angeles Rams and Sean McVay at the end of the 2022 season after L.A. finished with a win/loss record of 5-12. 2022 was McVay’s only losing season with the […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 13: Head coach Sean McVay and offensive coordinator Liam Coen of the Los Angeles Rams on the field before a preseason game against the Los Angeles Charger at SoFi Stadium on August 13, 2022 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images) | Getty Images Liam Coen was on The Pivot Podcast when he spoke about one of his biggest coaching regrets, and it boiled down to Coen leaving the Los Angeles Rams and Sean McVay at the end of the 2022 season after L.A. finished with a win/loss record of 5-12. 2022 was McVay’s only losing season with the Rams to this point, and according to Coen, perhaps their most challenging year as a coach at any level. Coen, with hindsight, looks back at leaving the Rams and choosing to go to Kentucky as their offensive coordinator as the easier of the two choices. Despite how hard it may have been for Coen to stay in L.A. at the time, he thinks he would’ve learned more had he stuck with McVay and the Rams to help them navigate past their down ‘22 season. Whereas the Rams finished 2022 on a low note, and McVay wasn’t even sure how much longer he’d stay with the team, the next season, in 2023, McVay and the Rams turned things around as they bounced back with a 10-7 campaign before losing to the Detroit Lions in the playoffs. Coen missed out on the dramatic turnaround, and all the lessons that would’ve come with it. It’s unclear exactly what Coen would want to change about his past as he reflects that everything worked out well for him as he did take the position at Kentucky, then took a position with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in 2024 before becoming the head coach of the Jacksonville Jaguars in 2025. Perhaps he simply regrets missing out on the learning experience that McVay and the rest of the Rams went through between the 2022 and 2023 season. You can see Coen’s response below and judge for yourself. “‘Kevin O’Connell is going to get the Vikings job; I’d love for you to come back as the OC’…I’m like ‘I can’t pass that up’. And it ends up being our hardest year, and the most challenging year. And that was probably one of my biggest regrets. In this profession you ask about movements and what goes into that. Sean at that time in ‘22 we had that tough year, won 5 games, and weren’t really quite sure what he (Sean) was gonna do maybe in ways? And Kentucky called back, and we had just loved it there…kinda chasing money a little bit and also an ego decision. I wasn’t calling plays in L.A…not just calling plays but leading…and that was my biggest regret going back to Kentucky in 2023…because you know what? I thought it was an opportunity…to stick something out with a friend and an organization that gave you your first opp (opportunity) that I missed, that I walked away from when it was hard…I had some regret…did work out in the end, but it was my biggest regret of moves in my career.” Coen found success with Jacksonville in his first year as HC, leading them to a playoff spot. His Jags will now look to go even deeper into the playoffs in 2026 as the expectations for Coen are likely the highest they’ve been in his career. Though things did work out for Coen, he’s perhaps reflecting that the best coaches learn by navigating hardships, not running from them. Coen didn’t do anything wrong; he had a chance to go elsewhere in a position he wanted and he took it with Kentucky. Would Coen be a better coach today had he stayed with the Rams? Seems like Coen wonders that. Either way, Coen doesn’t have to worry about bouncing back from a losing season in Jacksonville, not yet, but he will have to continue to meet the high expectations that his team have setup for themselves. And if he fails to meet those high expectations, then Coen may wind up with more regrets from his time in Jacksonville, than from his time in Los Angeles.

title: Matthew Stafford ranked 1st on controversial top-10 list
summary: As the reigning MVP, Matthew Stafford is no stranger to being called the best quarterback in the NFL right now, but maybe the order behind him is up for debate. Dave Portnoy released his top-10 quarterbacks list on Monday and the L.A. Rams’ QB was first, unsurprisingly, but Lamar Jackson was nowhere to be found. […]
full_text: LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 1: Matthew Stafford #9 of the Los Angeles Rams throws during training camp at Loyola Marymount University on August 1, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images As the reigning MVP, Matthew Stafford is no stranger to being called the best quarterback in the NFL right now, but maybe the order behind him is up for debate. Dave Portnoy released his top-10 quarterbacks list on Monday and the L.A. Rams’ QB was first, unsurprisingly, but Lamar Jackson was nowhere to be found. Instead, Portnoy had names like Caleb Williams and Jayden Daniels above Joe Burrow, and Jalen Hurts above Lamar and Dak Prescott. Could you agree with this list as it is: The TOP 10 QBs in the NFL right now, ranked by Dave Portnoy 👀 Thoughts?! 🧐 pic.twitter.com/Sb3Xtf87pm — DraftKings (@DraftKings) August 17, 2026 Even Drake Maye above Josh Allen is flat out incorrect, but Portnoy is a Patriots fan. Where the top-10 is wrong In my opinion. Maye is going to experience a fall from near-MVP this season unless he gets dramatically better with A.J. Brown. His stats were inflated last season and then New England was gifted a trip to the Super Bowl with one of the easiest playoff schedules of modern times. Allen should be top-2. Patrick Mahomes is a three-time Super Bowl winner, so it’s fair to give him the benefit of the doubt after returning from his injury. Caleb Williams had easily one of the most overrated quarterback seasons in the last 20 years. He also needs to get better, not just climb out of holes that he dug for himself. Jayden Daniels was not very good last season and that was before the injury. His recent publicity for going after LSU for “disrespecting” him has not helped his case. MLB teams have been trolling Jayden Daniels: pic.twitter.com/jKgLfR4pC1 — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) August 16, 2026 Burrow has things to clean up in his game and he does get help from his supporting cast, he also needs to stay healthy. But he’s a lot better than Caleb and Jayden. He’s also probably better than Maye. Hurts? Nothing needs to be said. Sam Darnold is riding on the high of the Super Bowl, same as Hurts apparently, and his NFC Championship performance against the Rams definitely earned him some points given how poorly had he played against L.A. before then. But he’s entering the prove-it season now. Jordan Love? Well, I don’t even consider 10th to be that high. It’s a very debatable position no matter who is there. Although Lamar Jackson does get overrated too, he’s certainly better than a few names on this list. Do you agree or think this one got it just right?
