title: 49ers 53-man roster projection:  Stocking up on pass rushers and cutting 1 rookie
summary: There’s nothing better than overreacting to a preseason game — a preseason game where the majority of San Francisco 49ers starters sat out, nonetheless. Football is fluid, and a decision that you felt strongly about last Wednesday could be completely different by Saturday. That’s what the coaching staff is dealing with daily after every practice. […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 13: Romello Height #94 of the San Francisco 49ers looks on from the sideline against the Tennessee Titans in the second half at Levi's Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images There’s nothing better than overreacting to a preseason game — a preseason game where the majority of San Francisco 49ers starters sat out, nonetheless. Football is fluid, and a decision that you felt strongly about last Wednesday could be completely different by Saturday. That’s what the coaching staff is dealing with daily after every practice. Here is an updated 53-man roster projection heading into the second week of the preseason. Quarterback (3): Brock Purdy, Mac Jones, Kurtis Rourke Nobody had Rourke making the roster when camp started. Then we saw him operate Kyle Shanahan’s offense with only two starters. Rourke is likely Purdy’s backup for the next couple of seasons after Jones leaves in free agency next offseason. The 49ers aren’t going to risk losing their future backup who has two seasons remaining on his rookie contract after 2026 on waivers. Running backs (4): Christian McCaffrey, Kyle Juszczyk, Jordan James, Kaelon Black This position seems relatively cut and dry. I have Isaac Guerendo beginning the season on the PUP list as of now. The running backs who played in the first preseason game are the definition of camp bodies. If there’s another injury before Week 1, or one of the James/Black duo isn’t healthy, expect Patrick Taylor Jr. to be the next man up due to his special teams experience. Wide Receiver (6): Mike Evans, De’Zhaun Stribling, Deebo Samuel, Demarcus Robinson, Jordan Watkins, Jacob Cowing That sixth spot is up for grabs, as the first five are set in stone. There isn’t a single reason to keep Christian Kirk if he misses the entire camp. The 49ers gave him $1.6 million guaranteed this offseason. Kirk turns 30 in November. I have a hard time imagining teams rushing to sign him when they had the opportunity in March and didn’t. I can’t quit Cowing. The 49ers will if he suffers another injury at any point over the next couple of weeks. Cowing reportedly got banged up again during Sunday’s practice, but returned to action and made plays. His speed is real and unlike anything else on the roster. He is also the best returner on the roster. None of that matters if Cowing can’t stay on the field, which he has proven he can’t to this point. Still, he brings something to the table that has been missing in this offense, which is why his leash continues to be long. Tight end (3): George Kittle, Jake Tonges, Luke Farrell Kittle said he’ll return sooner than late r. I believe him. Even if it’s not Week 1, he might use that time to get into football shape and be back by Week 2 or 3. If there’s any inkling of Kittle playing within the first month, you don’t place him on the PUP. You can use the other two on special teams, which might help you skim at other positions. The 49ers working out undrafted free agent Khalil Dinkins this past weekend was their way of telling us how they feel about the tight ends behind these three. Offensive line (9): Trent Williams, Vederian Lowe, Robert Jones, Carver Willis, Jake Brendel, Brett Toth, Dominick Puni, Colton McKivitz, Connor Colby There’s great risk entering the season with one backup tackle. However, McKivitz hasn’t missed a game since 2022. The 49ers would be banking on history here. Enrique Cruz Jr. doesn’t look like he knows what he’s doing. Based on what he put on film last Thursday, it’d be surprising if another team claimed him. Who knows how the guard rotation will work, so I’d expect the Niners to roster several. If Jones and Willis run away are a tier above Colby, don’t be surprised if the team signs a tackle off waivers and parts ways with Colby. Remember, he’s a seventh-round pick from last year. His spot isn’t guaranteed, and it shouldn’t be. Defensive line(10): Nick Bosa, Osa Odighizuwa, Alfred Collins, Romello Height, CJ West, Keion White, Gracen Halton, Sam Okuayinonu, Bryson Eason, Ogbo Okoronkwo It seems like the 49ers have their minds made up at EDGE. I’m taking an extra pass rusher with Mykel Williams presumably beginning the season on the PUP. The 49ers add a veteran who could give you 10-15 snaps, which might not seem like a big deal, but that’s the difference in keeping Bosa fresh or Height off the field for run downs. The final spot along the defensive line is a battle between Eason, James Thompson Jr., and Sebastian Valdez. Valdez’s upper body strength and agility will make this competition close. But Eason’s compact frame, lower-body explosiveness, and technique that let him hold up against double teams and win 1-on-1 as a run defender make him too valuable to cut. He’s the type of moldable clay Kris Kocurek should be working with daily. Linebacker (6): Fred Warner, Dre Greenlaw, Jaden Dugger, Tatum Bethune, Luke Gifford, Nick Martin If I were making the rules, I’d punt on the third-rounder from 2025 and move forward with either Garret Wallow or Larry Worth III. Martin looks like he’s behind the 8-ball when it comes to knowing the ins and outs of linebacker play. The only way for him to get better is to play, but that’s not going to happen if he performs anything like he did last Thursday. The fact that he was taken off the field on obvious passing downs was not a good look. Dugger is too intriguing a prospect to move on from. I wouldn’t be surprised if he starts as the third linebacker, or even comes into the game if Raheem Morris has doubts about Greenlaw’s coverage ability. Gifford sticks for special teams reasons and because of a $1.35 million guaranteed salary. Cornerback (5): Deommodore Lenoir, Renardo Green, Upton Stout, Jack Jones, Ephesians Prysock Goodnight, Darrell Luter Jr. He was making similar mistakes in the preseason that he made as a rookie. Prysock can do all of the things you ask of Luter Jr., and you get him for four years on a rookie deal, as opposed to Luter Jr., who is in the final year of his contract. Nate Hobbs missing “a few weeks” with a groin injury likely seals his fate. If anything happens to Stout at nickel, you can bump Lenoir inside and play Jones on the outside. Jakob Robinson likely sticks on the practice squad and continues to sharpen his skills in the slot. Safety(4): Malik Mustapha, Ji’Ayir Brown, Marques Sigle, Ashtyn Davis Davis has played himself onto the roster. He had a near interception and took on an offensive lineman blocking at full speed. Those two plays were impressive. Siran Neal is 32 and in the final season of his contract. If he added any value at safety, he’d be in the discussion, but that’s clearly not the case. Davis is also a couple of years younger than Neal and was with Brant Boyer on the Jets. Watching the safety rotation throughout the season should be a rollercoaster. I’m still not convinced Sigle is the answer. But I’ve seen Mustapha and Brown make similar mistakes by allowing deep passes to go over their heads. Maybe Davis gets a shot to play at some point. Realistically, the Niners would find an answer on the waiver wire at the end of the month or at some point ahead of the trade deadline if they feel like they aren’t getting the type of production Raheem Morris wants at the position. Special teams (3): K Eddy Pineiro, P Corliss Waitman, LS Jon Weeks The 49ers kept the lefty at punter and were rewarded with a muff in the preseason. Jack Bouwmeester will be stashed on the Rams as an International Pathway Program Exemption.
author: Kyle Posey

title: 49ers coordinator reveals competition that is getting ‘harder and harder’ to call
summary: In under two weeks time, the 49ers will need to cut their roster to 53 players ahead of the 2026 NFL season. That is always a challenging and brutal task for any team as the general manager and head coach are given the unfortunate job of dashing the hopes of a host of players. Heading […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - AUGUST 13: Gracen Halton #93 of the San Francisco 49ers tackles Tyjae Spears #2 of the Tennessee Titans during the game at Levi's Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. The Titans defeated the 49ers 19-13. (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images In under two weeks time, the 49ers will need to cut their roster to 53 players ahead of the 2026 NFL season. That is always a challenging and brutal task for any team as the general manager and head coach are given the unfortunate job of dashing the hopes of a host of players. Heading into another season where they again have aspirations of emerging from a formidable NFC West and contending for the Super Bowl, the tough decisions that come with putting together a 53-man roster and practice squad take on an added pertinence for the 49ers. And one position that is seemingly set to give the 49ers a headache as they construct their roster is the defensive tackle spot. It is a position that has been area of concern for the Niners for the last three seasons, and San Francisco has invested significant resources into turning things around at that spot. This year, there is reason for optimism, with the 49ers having traded for a skilled interior pass rusher in Osa Odighizuwa while acquiring a pair of rookies who have shone early. Fourth-round pick Gracen Halton and undrafted free agent Bryson Eason both impressed in the 49ers’ preseason opener against the Tennessee Titans, Halton registering a sack in which he beat veteran guard Peter Skoronski, while Eason caught the eye with his play against the run. Sebastian Valdez, a UDFA last year who spent 2025 on the practice squad, boosted his claim for a spot on the active roster by registering five tackles, including one for a loss. Their performances came as last year’s second-round pick Alfred Collins struggled and with 2025 fourth-round pick C.J. West on the sideline due to an unspecified injury. And, when asked about West in a press conference on Sunday, defensive coordinator Raheem Morris indicated the fight for places on the depth chart at defensive tackle is getting increasingly difficult to judge. “He’s done some really good things. C.J. ultimately coming here, let’s be honest, he came in, he’s seen a big-time run stopper and a guy that can really hold up, particularly towards the end of the season to do some things in that nose tackle position, so to speak. And then when I got here, I seen he had more quickness than he had when he first got here, and he’s gotten better and better throughout the process. To see him be able to spike and do different movements to get to the backfield and cause pass rush and cause disruption, whether it be our first team, second team, whatever team’s out there, watching him do those things. Had his little, small setback, obviously missing a couple days, but he’s been back out there in the mix. So, I’m really fired up to see where he goes from here and what he’s able to do and how he can contribute to that line. All of those guys create such a competition right now, and that’s what you want. You don’t want it to be easy for us to be able to pick out a football team, and I just think they’re making it harder and harder every day.” It would be unrealistic to expect the 49ers to carry more than five defensive tackles on the active roster this season. As such, the emergence of Halton, Eason and Valdez places pressure on Collins and West to impress and lock down their spots. West, despite his absence, is better equipped to do so. While neither West nor Collins are known for their pass-rushing ability, West is the player with more potential in that area, as Morris articulated. Given his comparative lack of tools when getting after the quarterback, Collins could find himself in significant trouble if he cannot produce better play against the run. It is important to note that Collins has only recently returned to the field from shoulder surgery, which could go some way to explaining his struggles. Still, with others impressing and the 49ers viewed as a possible landing spot for veteran defensive tackle Vita Vea, neither Collins nor West can be considered a lock for the roster at a position that will be fascinating to watch over the course of the final two preseason games.
author: Nicholas McGee

title: 49ers News: Can’t wait to see Kittle back
summary: Tight end Jake Tonges, a former tech bro, on ‘full-circle moment’ after $8 million contract with 49ers (paywall)“The 49ers run a lot of 22-personnel formations, or in other words, sets with two tight ends. On paper, Tonges is a prototypical receiving tight end and Farrell is known for his blocking. First-year tight ends coach Cam […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - AUGUST 13: George Kittle #85 of the San Francisco 49ers walks on the field before a preseason NFL game against the Tennessee Titans on August 13, 2026 at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara, CA. (Photo by Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Tight end Jake Tonges, a former tech bro, on ‘full-circle moment’ after $8 million contract with 49ers (paywall) “The 49ers run a lot of 22-personnel formations, or in other words, sets with two tight ends. On paper, Tonges is a prototypical receiving tight end and Farrell is known for his blocking. First-year tight ends coach Cam Clemmons has tried to help them out of those boxes. Clemmons, previously an assistant offensive line coach for the 49ers, has been especially helpful to Tonges. “That’s been my challenge to him, is, Jake, your ceiling isn’t last year,” Clemmons said. “Last year was just kind of the beginning.” Key 49ers position battle remains undecided heading into preseason Week 2 “Wide receiver Jacob Cowing had a couple of hard falls during practice, the second of which resulted in a diving reception on a deep pass from Purdy. Cowing had a couple of steps on cornerback Deommodore Lenoir, and he laid out to catch the 45-yard downfield throw. Earlier, Cowing and Marques Sigle took hard spills after they both went up for a Purdy pass along the left side of the field.“ 49ers’ George Kittle eyes return to practice, opener in Australia “For most of the process, Kittle said he has had to focus on doing as many seated and standing calf raises as possible every day. His workouts, however, have taken on a more football-specific approach of late. As the Niners practiced last week, Kittle was running and cutting at nearly full speed while running routes and catching passes from a team staffer on a side field. On Sunday, Kittle said he’s hitting the speed benchmarks set for him on the GPS and is “pretty close” to hitting the same speed numbers he hit before the injury. Kittle said he has a target date in mind for returning to practice but declined to share it. He added that he’s “very confident” he won’t start the season on the physically unable to perform list, meaning he intends to be back within the season’s first four games.“ 49ers OC Klay Kubiak shares updates on Rourke, Stribling, Evans, Kittle, and Purdy “”There’s a time and a place, but you want the mindset to drive the football, and Brock has both tools, and Brock is exceptional at whatever layering it is. Throwing it over, zoning defenders, finding holes in the defense, he’s exceptional at that. But you want the mindset as a quarterback, ‘I’m driving the football.’ We remind him of that, and he has both tools. So, I think the nickname’s funny, I appreciate it, but it’s cool that Brock kind of takes it personally, too, and says, ‘No, I’m going to drive the ball. I’m not going to layer things.’ But you got to have both tools in your bag. So, it’s kind of a funny deal between him and Raheem.” The Good and Not So Good from Day 13 of 49ers Camp: Mike Evans Dominates (Finally) “He still doesn’t create a ton of separation against man coverage, but neither does Evans. Both receivers are excellent at catching passes over the heads of defensive backs. And Stribling in particular is fearless when it comes to running full speed across the field. It looks like he’s being groomed to start this season, considering he’s not playing any special teams. As opposed to Deebo Samuel, who’s a punt returner and a kick returner. And when he plays with the starters, he mostly is a running back.” 49ers 53-man roster projection (paywall) “The 49ers probably have to keep five, and if we’re talking about the best 53, all seven of these players should make the team. James Thompson Jr. has an abundance of untapped upside, but he’s not polished. Valdez has certainly done enough to earn a spot, but he’s not consistent. Eason, meanwhile, is an imperious force who can hold up against double teams. He’s a Day 1 NFL-caliber player. Everyone else is a no-brainer.“ George Kittle expects to return to the 49ers ‘sooner than later’ “I’ve been running around a lot. Hitting top speeds. Hopefully, we’re back in pads practicing sooner than later. Just trying to check the boxes and not be a dumbass is what I would say. Kittle said he spoke with Richard Sherman about the rehab process of an Achilles injury. He said building a strong foundation after the next eight weeks is the most important part: “If you build a strong foundation, get your calf muscle back, get your strength back, then you’re allowed to train faster and get your body ready to go faster. So, we dominated those 8 weeks. Had a really good rehab.” Kittle mentioned how a Week 1 target date made it easy to light a fire under him. He said he was doing seated calf raises within ten minutes of taking his cast off. Kittle said he’s hitting the numbers that he needs to hit as far as the GPS times and markers go. Kittle understands that he needs to practice before he plays: “I don’t want my first time in pads traveling to Australia. I don’t think that’d be a very smart idea. These next couple of weeks are everything. That’ll let me know whether I’m able to play Week 1 or not.”

title: Buccaneers roster 2026: Yaya Diaby, Alex Anzalone, and Keionte Scott are underrated
summary: The 2026 Tampa Bay Buccaneers are a very interesting team, because there’s no way to know if what happened in 2025 will lead to a reload or a rebuild. Starting with Baker Mayfield’s situation. In his first two seasons with the Bucs after signing a one-year, $4 million contract in 2023, and following that up […]
full_text: The 2026 Tampa Bay Buccaneers are a very interesting team, because there’s no way to know if what happened in 2025 will lead to a reload or a rebuild. Starting with Baker Mayfield’s situation. In his first two seasons with the Bucs after signing a one-year, $4 million contract in 2023, and following that up with a three-year, $100 million deal with $40 million guaranteed in 2024, things went about as well as anyone could expect. In 2023 and 2024 combined , Mayfield finished: Third in the league in passing attempts (1,136) Third in completions (771) Second in passing yards (8,544) First in passing touchdowns (69) First in interceptions (26 — yes, this is a problem); and Seventh in quarterback rating (100.7). 2025 looked like a continuation of the two prior seasons, until it didn’t — for all kinds of reasons, Mayfield’s season split cleanly in two from an efficiency perspective, as the Bucs finished 8-9 after starting the season 6-2. The splits, per Sumer Sports : First Half (Weeks 1-9): Attempts: 269 Completions: 172 (63.9%) Yards: 1,919 Yards per Attempt: 7.13 Touchdowns: 13 (4.8% TD rate) Interceptions: 2 (0.7% INT rate) EPA per Attempt: 0.161 Average Depth of Target: 8.6 yards Second Half (Weeks 10-18): Attempts: 274 Completions: 171 (62.4%) Yards: 1,774 Yards per Attempt: 6.47 Touchdowns: 13 (4.7% TD rate) Interceptions: 9 (3.3% INT rate) EPA per Attempt: 0.057 Average Depth of Target: 7.5 yards This was not all Mayfield’s fault. The 2025 Bucs had nine different offensive line combinations, and most of his primary weapons — receivers Mike Evans, Chris Godwin, and Jalen McMillan, as well as running back Bucky Irving — all missed serious time. And Evans, who may be in the Hall of Fame when all is said and done, is of course now with the San Francisco 49ers. This has led to all sorts of agita regarding Mayfield’s future with the team. His current contract is set to void on February 16, 2027 , and right now, talks regarding an extension have stalled . If Mayfield goes elsewhere next season, Tampa Bay will likely need to replace him in either free agency or the draft, as the current depth chart of Jake Browning, Connor Bazelak, and Jalon Daniels probably isn’t going to scare the rest of the NFL anytime soon. So, a team that hasn’t advanced further than the Divisional Round of the playoffs since Tom Brady and a suffocating defense led it to a win in Super Bowl LV at the end of the 2020 season could be looking at another sea change sooner than later. In the interim, if these Bucs want to get back to the postseason after narrowly missing out in 2025, it’ll take everyone pulling together — not just the stars, but also (perhaps especially) the guys whose on-field exploits have not yet presented them with the national recognition they deserve. To that end, I’ve identified three Hidden Gems for the 2026 Buccaneers — one underrated veteran, one underrated free-agent signing, and one underrated rookie. Underrated veteran: DL Yaya Diaby One player who is on the verge of stardom in this defense is Yaya Diaby, the 2023 third-round pick out of Louisville who has been quite the pressure machine in his NFL career, and is starting to get the sacks to match. Diaby actually had nine sacks with just 30 pressures in his rookie year, and he matched that sack total last season with 62 pressures. “We thought he was one of our best pass rushers, and the best at the time,” head coach Todd Bowles said of Diaby’s 2025 season in February . “He had more pressures than everybody; he just didn’t finish them. We thought he became a much better player. He wasn’t thinking as much, and some of his sacks, it could have easily turned into being a 15-sack year. He is playing his tail off, and he works at it. So really, the way he played, you didn’t have the result that you want, but the way he played was unbelievable.” I’d be less likely to split hairs with the nature of Diaby’s play last season — he also had 33 solo tackles, 33 stops, 13 tackles for loss, and a forced fumble — but when you consider that Bowles now has Rueben Bain to add to the defensive front, perhaps Diaby’s efforts will be thusly magnified. Regardless, if there’s a next level for Yaya Diaby, he appears to be right on the precipice of it. Todd Bowles has said that he would like to see Yaya Diaby close on all those pressures he gets, and turn them into more sacks. I can see that happening in 2026. Dude is relentless. pic.twitter.com/4cUHXNPqGm — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 14, 2026 Underrated free agent: LB Alex Anzalone Big changes are coming to Tampa Bay’s linebacker corps with the retirement of future Hall of Famer Lavonte David. Second-round rookie Josiah Trotter should get a lot of starting reps, and the Bucs signed former New Orleans Saints and Detroit Lions ‘backer Alex Anzalone to a two-year, $17 million contract with $12 million guaranteed. Not a bad deal for a guy who, in 2025, had 68 solo tackles, 44 stops, three sacks, 18 total pressures, and four tackles for loss. Perhaps most importantly for what Bowles will want him to do, Anzalone allowed 40 catches on 61 targets for 409 yards, 156 yards after the catch, two touchdowns, one interception, seven pass breakups, and an opponent passer rating of 88.8. “He has a more complex system than what I am used to, but it has been pretty easy to pick up and communicate and understand what he is trying to accomplish,” Anzalone recently said of Bowles’ defense , and his role within it. “I think the biggest thing for me as a linebacker is trying to see what he likes to call in certain situations and understanding him as a play-caller as opposed to the actual playbook. “You look at mismatches that offenses look for, and a lot of tight ends around the league they look at, because of their size. When you get a safety covering them, they obviously have the size advantage. Me being a longer, athletic linebacker, I am able to do that role, and I know now that I am going to be asked to do a little bit more than I have in the past and it is a benefit – God-given.” The tape doesn’t lie in this case. Anzalone can provide legitimate coverage everywhere from the box to outside cornerback leverage. Alex Anzalone covering running backs and tight ends all over the place. He'll be doing a lot of this for the @Buccaneers . pic.twitter.com/UYvA1GZqiv — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 14, 2026 Every defense needs a green dot guy in the middle of it, and while Anzalone certainly isn’t Lavonte David in his prime, he has the capacity to make this contract look like a massive bargain when he’s at his best. Underrated draft pick: DB Keionte Scott I almost put Georgia State receiver Ted Hurst here, because I became a big fan in the pre-draft process , but when the Bucs took Miami defensive back Keionte Scott with the 116th pick in the fourth round… well, that was going to be my guy. I would have taken Scott a lot higher, based on his play and playing personality, and I really don’t care that he’s 5’11¼ and 193 pounds. Where does Miami CB Keionte Scott's 4.33 speed show up? Everywhere. Closing to the ball on a blitz or for a TFL, at the top of the route stem when he's recovering, and from sideline to sideline. Love his playing personality. This guy is feisty as hell. pic.twitter.com/1Cb5vyQIbB — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) March 30, 2026 Last season for the NCAA runners-up, Scott allowed 39 catches on 56 targets for 332 yards, 214 yards after the catch, no touchdowns, two interceptions, five pass breakups, and an opponent passer rating of 69.9. Scott also had five sacks, 20 total pressures, five tackles for loss, two forced fumbles, 51 solo tackles, and 36 stops. Basically, everything you want a modern cornerback to do, Scott can do it — he just can’t be 6’1”. “Yeah, we’re going to look at him [at outside cornerback],” Bowles said of Scott in May . “We’ve got to move our guys around, because when you make cuts, you don’t have that many. We’ve got to be able to have some…

title: Tampa Bay Buccaneers news: A win, but mixed results vs. Jets
summary: The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are 1-0 in the preseason after beating the New York Jets 24-16, but they may not have played their best football. The Bucks trailed 10-0 at the end of the first quarter, but they found a way to rally back and pull out an eight-point victory. Bucs Nation, how do you […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - AUGUST 14: Brady Cook #4 of the New York Jets runs the ball in the third quarter against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at MetLife Stadium on August 14, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Evan Bernstein/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are 1-0 in the preseason after beating the New York Jets 24-16, but they may not have played their best football. The Bucks trailed 10-0 at the end of the first quarter, but they found a way to rally back and pull out an eight-point victory. Bucs Nation, how do you feel about the preseason opener? Let us know in the comments section below. Today’s Buccaneers news Grading The Buccaneers After Their 24-16 Preseason Win Against The Jets | Tampa Bay Buccaneers On SI The Tampa Bay Buccaneers performed well against the New York Jets in their preseason opener, but there’s still a lot of room for improvement. The best group during the game was the team’s defensive backs, who helped produce a pair of turnovers, including one that went for a pick-six. Bucs Must Improve Fast On Special Teams After Stumbling vs. Jets | Pewter Report The Buccaneers’ special teams unit did not put up their best performance against the Jets. Special teams coordinator Danny Smith is widely respected, but the NFL is a “what have you done for me lately?” kind of league. title: Titans have the offensive line problem we all knew they had
summary: The Tennessee Titans won their first preseason game, defeating the San Francisco 49ers 19-13. Despite the victory, the general reaction from the fanbase has been one of concern. Quarterback Cam Ward struggled, completing less than 50% of his passes. One positive was the performance of the starting offensive line. Ward was rarely under duress. Rookie […]
full_text: Tennessee Titans center Pat Coogan (79) and tackle Austin Deculus (76) run drills during mandatory minicamp at Vanderbilt Health Football Center in Nashville, Tenn., Wednesday, June 17, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Tennessee Titans won their first preseason game, defeating the San Francisco 49ers 19-13 . Despite the victory, the general reaction from the fanbase has been one of concern. Quarterback Cam Ward struggled, completing less than 50% of his passes. One positive was the performance of the starting offensive line. Ward was rarely under duress. Rookie Fernando Carmona has surprisingly emerged as the favorite to win the starting right guard job. Once the depth linemen entered the game, the Titans’ weaknesses were exposed. We’ve especially been beating the drum about the swing offensive tackle spots behind starters Dan Moore Jr. and JC Latham. Austin Deculus played second-string left tackle and was downright abysmal. Pro Football Focus credited him with allowing two sacks and slapped him with a score of 19.0 in pass protection. If there was a positive, it was that sophomore UDFA Brandon Crenshaw-Dickson was pretty steady at right tackle. Are the Titans going to trust Crenshaw-Dickson to play behind both Moore and Latham though? General manager Mike Borgonzi needs to strongly consider finding a creative way to get better at the No. 3 tackle spot. Carmona has emerged as the likely starting right guard partially because the initial contenders have disappointed. Veteran Cordell Volson entered the game and struggled both in pass protection and as a run blocker. Jackson Slater played exclusively at left guard, where he’s listed on the depth chart as Peter Skoronski’s backup. Slater was also tagged with allowing a sack by PFF. If Carmona wasn’t trending in an interesting decision, the Titans would probably be forced to make a move at guard (Kevin Zeitler?). Elsewhere, they should absolutely consider a transaction at swing tackle, where Deculus is already predictably falling on his face. The first week of the preseason proved the Titans have the offensive line issues we knew they did.

title: How Commanders preseason win vs. Dolphins influenced key position battles
summary: The Commanders entered training camp with several key position battles needing resolution.   One has come early. Washington sided with Drew Stevens in the kicker competition, a point made clear by Jake Moody’s reported release on Monday afternoon. That made the undrafted rookie out of Iowa the choice, assuming Stevens continues playing well and no […]
full_text: The Commanders entered training camp with several key position battles needing resolution. One has come early. Washington sided with Drew Stevens in the kicker competition, a point made clear by Jake Moody’s reported release on Monday afternoon. That made the undrafted rookie out of Iowa the choice, assuming Stevens continues playing well and no other competition is added. There are several unsettled position battles on this roster, though Friday night’s preseason game had some influence on them. Let’s reexamine the state of a few roster spots following that 20-7 victory over the Miami Dolphins at Northwest Stadium. Running back The Commanders might have a tough time deciding how to round out their running back room. Bill Croskey-Merritt and Rachaad White are obviously the top options, with sixth-rounder Kaytron Allen firmly in the mix. Veteran Jeremy McNichols will be out a few weeks dealing with a quadriceps injury , which kept him out of Friday’s game and a series of future practices. Jerome Ford returned the first kickoff, but didn’t play much. That created an opportunity for undrafted rookie Robert Henry Jr., who took full advantage . The former Texas-San Antonio back took full advantage, with 75 yards and a touchdown on 12 carries. He’s an explosive playmaker who quickly became a fan camp crush and is someone we need to see more of in the preseason. Can he protect the passer? Can he contribute well on special teams. The Commanders need all of that from a fourth running back. While McNichols is out a little while, he’s also a proven commodity. That will keep him firmly in the mix despite his injury. Center Nick Allegretti is set to return to practice on Tuesday. That’s a positive development for a position that has been without its starter since the first camp practice. Top reserve Julian Good-Jones has struggled some in camp, and there’s some video of him getting beat during Friday night’s game. Good-Jones gets completely BLOWN UP by a Dolphins LB on a blitz pic.twitter.com/nMh3sQWrbO — Tiller56 (Hogs Haven) (@Tiller56) August 15, 2026 Our Mark Tyler also found evidence of Matt Gulbin playing well at center as a pass protector and a quality blocker in the second level. Quinn praised Gulbin’s performance during a Sunday press conference , and also said he’ll get some reps at guard to round out his versatility as a 2026 depth piece. Allegretti’s still your starter at center. His direct backup seems up in the air at this point, with Gulbin’s performance making it possible he could end up in the No. 2 spot on the depth chart. Safety Quan Martin had a solid game on Friday, parterning with Will Harris at the safety spot early in Friday’s game. He played a bit more than expected for someone who has played prominently over the past two seasons, but he’s locked in a position battle with veteran Jeremy Reaves. Quinn intimated that Reaves and three-down starter Nick Cross could be featured in a Week 2 preseason game at Detroit, allowing the staff to compare and contrast their options at safety. Quan coming downhill like a 🦇 out of HELL to make the big hit!!! pic.twitter.com/OKEHRODgA0 — Tiller56 (Hogs Haven) (@Tiller56) August 15, 2026 Martin looked good on Friday, but he’ll have to maintain that level of play to fight off Reaves. Martin was often a liability last season — he had a 155 passer rating allowed when targeted in 2025 — and the Commanders need better from the safety position overall in 2026. Cross will provide that, but he needs a running mate that’s solid in coverage and playing deep. Martin’s game play was decent. Let’s see how Reaves responds when he’s given game reps. Quarterback Marcus Mariota suffered a right MCL sprain early in Friday’s game, leaving most of the work to Sam Hartman and Athan Kaliakmanis. Expect that trend to continue, with Mariota set to miss the entire preseason and Quinn stating the Commanders don’t anticiapte adding another quarterback. Jayden Daniels is the unquestioned starter and Mariota is his backup, but the Commanders will keep one developmental third quarterback. Which guy will win that spot? Kaliakmanis showed better on Friday, showcasing solid arm talent. Hartman was inefficient and had some big misses and an interception that showed lackluster decision making. Both quarterbacks must be better to take the lead in the race for QB3. The receivers need them on point as well, as they try to stand out and make the plays required to earn a roster spot. It will be interesting to see which quarterback takes second-team reps with Mariota out. That will be our first clue in who has the lead coming out of Friday. Based on that game, it should be Kaliakmanis. Wide Receiver Stefon Diggs complicated the receiver depth chart in the best possible way, adding proven, dynamic production to the No. 2 receiver spot. The Commanders have options with how to complete the group and the roles within it. Rookie Antonio Williams is expected to be the third option prominently featured in the slot, but it was mildly notable that he didn’t enter Friday’s game until the third quarter, well after others got their shot. Jaylin Lane caught some key passes. Treylon Burks was involved. Dyami Brown is sitting right there, and we haven’t even mentioned Luke McCaffrey yet. I just can’t see the Commanders keeping seven receivers, even with two of them as prominent returners and special teams players. Then there’s undrafted receiver Jaden Bradley. We need more time for these receivers to create separation and see which guy is performing in what role. Receivers made some nice plays, but it’s hard to say the first preseason game settled any arguments.

title: 2026 Fantasy Football Preview: Which Commanders players are draftable?
summary: First, a prefatory note. When debuting as Hogs Haven’s fantasy writer last year, I offered an introduction that talked about the wide variety of experience I have in playing different types of leagues, with a proud learning curve than began with Gus Frerotte as my first ever fantasy quarterback. Hand-in-hand with that tongue-in-cheek boast is […]
full_text: First, a prefatory note. When debuting as Hogs Haven’s fantasy writer last year, I offered an introduction that talked about the wide variety of experience I have in playing different types of leagues, with a proud learning curve than began with Gus Frerotte as my first ever fantasy quarterback. Hand-in-hand with that tongue-in-cheek boast is the explanation that I have no unique football insight(never even played!), but just a longstanding Washington fandom and passion for the game, such that all advice given ought to be taken with the appropriate grain of salt. Toward that end, I’m going to be providing my “cheat sheet” of positional rankings this year, but it’s worth a comment on what my process is and how to best use that info as a result. Every year, I stubbornly build my own spreadsheet of player projections before I look at a single other human’s rankings. The idea is to ensure that I’ve at least looked at the statistical history of every player I put on my draft board before I start to form a gut reaction about what they are worth. Usually, the result is some significant outliers that cause me to then have to circle back and question why I have a player rated either much higher or much lower than the consensus. And typically, I’ll end up adjusting my rankings back towards the consensus more often than not – but it helps me tease out places where I might actually be onto something or seeing a player to buy or fade differently than the default would suggest. In short, I wouldn’t take the cheat sheet here as gospel, by any stretch of the imagination. If you see Ladd McConkey (who I’m bullish on) over Emeka Egbuka (who many others are bullish on) and think that is nutty and incorrect – stick with your instincts. If I had the actual ability to accurately forecast the performance of 250+ draftable players down to the precise yard, I’d be betting on it in Vegas instead of typing into the void! (Heck, on draft day I’m sometimes liable to disagree with my own board – it’s one thing to put Kyren Williams over Jonathan Taylor when crunching numbers, but another entirely to actually pull the trigger if you come to that decision on the clock!) But if you see places on my cheet sheet where we are drastically different, those might be points to take a second look. If Jared Goff is QB20 on your board despite being much higher on mine, you might want to dig into the numbers and realize the guy has 4,438+ yards and 29+ TDs in four straight seasons before you completely write him off as replacement level. Running backs In 2025, young running backs were the story on draft day. From the highly touted Ashton Jeanty and Omarian Hampton, to late-round values like Jacory Croskey-Merritt and Kyle Monangai, new faces at the position reshaped the market and (especially in keeper and dynasty formats) provided options for fantasy players to take risks on talent at other positions early in their drafts with confidence they could fill in the rest of a competitive roster behind them. All together, there were nearly a dozen rookie running backs that played significant roles at some point in the season (see also: Sampson, Judkins, Skattebo, Marks, Harvey, Henderson). With only three running backs taken on the first three days of this April’s NFL draft, that will not be the case in 2026. Jerimiyah Love will be an instant starter at RB for the Cardinals, and Jadarian Price will have a chance to compete with Zach Charbonnet for headlining work in Seattle, but after that, it will take injuries or an unexpected emergence from late-round fliers for other rookies to have the same kind of relevance this season. (Keep an eye on Kaelon Black in San Francisco and Adam Randall in Baltimore as guys with no value in Week 1, but with a path to significant work behind elder statesmen of the position.) The practical effect of that market change is a late-middle round plateau in RB value. It’s still possible to build a team around prioritizing other positions – there are a number of elite WR options in particular likely to go early on draft day – but somewhere around Jadarian Price’s mid-7th round ESPN ADP, the choices thin considerably. Have enough starting RBs to roll with by that point in the draft, or take your chances hoping you can correctly predict a dominant fantasy performance from one of several backfields which instead look like time-shares (Harvey or Dobbins in Denver? Hubbard or Brooks in Carolina? Mason or Jones in Minnesota? Pollard or Spears in Tennessee?). WRs Getting More Love Meanwhile, there were more wide receivers taken in this year’s NFL draft than in any season since 2021. So while the top tier will still be irreplaceable – no one’s confusing late fliers for Ja’Marr Chase, Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Puka Nacua, or Amon-Ra St. Brown – there will be receivers to be found late that can sneakily provide flex or even WR2 value on a matchup-dependent basis this season. At the top, Jahmyr Gibbs and Bijan Robinson (not to be confused with former Commander and fellow “B. Robinson” on draft boards, Brian Robinson Jr.) will be the first duo off of most draft boards followed by a run on receivers (WR10 may be off a lot of draft boards before RB8). Brock Bowers, Tre McBride and Josh Allen will get a look from contrarians aiming to secure top QB or TE production starting in the late second round. And then it’s a familiar process from there – take the best players available on your board but try to draft in balanced fashion along the way (no taking your 5th RB before your 2nd WR, etc. – there’s little worse in fantasy than wasting talent on your bench that you’re stuck with because you can’t find a trade with the whole league knowing you’re more desperate to make a move than they are). Format and Variance in Fantasy Leagues Finally, a note about format and variance. If you read this mostly bi-weekly column last season, you were regularly reminded about the importance of your league settings in valuing your players. While that advice almost goes without saying, it is nevertheless true that, for example, the time to take quarterbacks on draft day will differ wildly in a 2 QB or superflex league (especially with 6-point passing TDs) than in a traditional 1 QB league (especially with 4-point passing Tds). In the latter, patience may be the recommended strategy at QB: Names like Nix, Mahomes, Stafford, and Goff are not even among the top-12 QBs options per the early August consensus rankings (via FantasyPros) and so there is a decent chance of there being at least one player you may like more than the majority of drafters who will linger well into the ninth round of your league. But in the former, there are only 32 NFL starting QB jobs to go around, a few of which are less than locked down for the season, and with as many as six teams not playing on certain bye weeks, there will be points in the season where all but two starting QBs across the league are needed for fantasy purposes, drastically increasing the value of dependable performers due to position scarcity. The same may be true of tweaks to your strategy if your league has all kinds of rules ranging from TD bonuses to points per reception to different types of defensive scoring. (In most leagues, I’d advise not to take a DST or a kicker until the final two picks, but in DST-premium scoring settings, there’s an argument for the Rams or Seahawks defenses once you have a starting lineup filled plus two or three bench RBs/WRs. In auction formats, nominating defenses early may be a way to draw money away from your actual targets!) Boom-or-Bust options Similarly, it bears repeating that for fantasy purposes a 7-7 season is exactly as useless as a 4-10 season. So when choosing between roughly equivalent players, there is reason to prefer a boom-or-bust option, that gives you the higher upside if everything breaks right. To build the core of your team, take the safe and consistent options in the early rounds. But to build your bench, swing for…

summary: The Commanders didn’t waste time resolving an important training camp position battle.   Washington will roll with rookie kicker Drew Stevens, a decision that was made clear when incumbent Jake Moody was released by the team, per a Monday afternoon report by Jordan Schultz.   This is likely to be confirmed after 4 p.m. ET […]

(Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Commanders didn’t waste time resolving an important training camp position battle. Washington will roll with rookie kicker Drew Stevens , a decision that was made clear when incumbent Jake Moody was released by the team, per a Monday afternoon report by Jordan Schultz. Sources: The #Commanders are releasing K Jake Moody. The 26-year-old went 19/23 on FGs last season, including 10/11 in Washington. He also made both of his 50+ yard attempts, with a long of 56 yards. pic.twitter.com/nl6BMFwGps — Jordan Schultz (@Schultz_Report) August 17, 2026 This is likely to be confirmed after 4 p.m. ET when NFL transactions are officially posted. Moody did not perform well during the last Commanders training camp block, with a few easy misses in practice. His last field-goal with the Commanders was a 29-yard volley in the first preseason game, played against the Dolphins, that doinked off the right upright but ultimately went through to add 3 point to the scoreboard. Stevens, in the same game, converted from 41 yards out and also hit a extra point moved back by a penalty. Moody was signed off Chicago’s practice squad last season and was the Commanders kicker from that point to the end of the 2025 season. He converted 91% of his field-goal attempts over six games, but Washington created competition by signing Stevens as an undrafted free agent ahead of OTAs. Stevens has a powerful leg and has proven accurate. Per Commanders radio host Grant Paulsen, Stevens was 43-of-48 in practice. He had one rough day – Moody also struggled then – but has been solid outside of that. Drew Stevens was 43/48 in practice and 1/1 in the preseason. Jake Moody was 36/47 in practice and 1/1 on a doink-make from 29 in the preseason. https://t.co/yPl3OOQWFE — Grant Paulsen (@GrantPaulsen) August 17, 2026 The Commanders have struggled to find consistency at the kicker position. They’re hoping Stevens can provide some stability at that spot following his standout career at Iowa. Stevens converted 80% of his field-goal attempts with the Hawkeyes, and hit 22-of-28 last season to lead the BigTen conference. He hit a 58-yarder in 2025, and has shown the ability to convert from distance that has become fairly routine for NFL kickers in recent seasons. title: Mason/Brennan Preseason Hype! Award: Who has the most hype after Week 1?
summary: Former Washington Redskins 6th-round draft pick Colt Brennan was a star in college at the University of Hawaii and brought that hype with him to Washington in 2008. Brennan was a cult sensation during his brief time here, and was the inspiration for the annual Mason/Brennan Preseason Hype! Awards here at Hogs Haven. Brennan passed […]
full_text: Aug 14, 2026; Landover, Maryland, USA; Washington Commanders running back Robert Henry Jr. (30) carries the ball to score a touchdown against the Miami Dolphins during the first half at Northwest Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Amber Searls-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Former Washington Redskins 6th-round draft pick Colt Brennan was a star in college at the University of Hawaii and brought that hype with him to Washington in 2008. Brennan was a cult sensation during his brief time here, and was the inspiration for the annual Mason/Brennan Preseason Hype! Awards here at Hogs Haven. Brennan passed away at the way-too-young age of 37 five years ago . This was started as a tongue-in-cheek tribute to players that fans push to the moon before they play a snap, or after one great performance in the preseason. But it also puts the focus on some of the unheralded players who fans hype up and have a fighter’s chance at making Washington’s roster. Colt Brennan was a great college player that lit up the preseason, but injuries and other issues saw him flame out in the NFL early. RIP Colt and thanks for the inspiration. The Rules: 1. Player must have been drafted late or signed by the Redskins as an undrafted free agent. Players that have only been on other teams practice squads that are signed by the team are also eligible. 2. A player that has been on the team for several years is still eligible if most of that time has been spent on the practice squad, inactive, or with very limited productivity/time The Keenan “the Barbarian” Robinson Amendment: only 6th-round draft picks or later for their first two years in the league. This is the third year of the Adam Peters/Dan Quinn era in Washington, and they are looking for a big rebound from last year’s disappointing 5-12 season. They entered last season with Super Bowl aspirations after getting to the NFC Championship Game in Year 1. Quinn replaced both his coordinators, and Peters worked on fixing the broken defense. Training camp opened last week, so it’s time for another round of the Mason/Brennan Preseason Hype! Awards to check in on who’s getting fans excited early. Last season saw Bill Croskey-Merritt turn from preseason hype monster, to winning the Pepsi Rookie of the Week Award four times last season. title: Commanders News: All-22 game film of Styles, Coleman, Henry and more
summary: The Daily Slop – 17 August 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Bullock’s Film Room […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MD - AUGUST 14: Washington Commanders center Matt Gulbin (66) blocks Miami Dolphins linebacker Jacob Rodriguez (10) while Washington Commanders running back Robert Henry Jr. (30) rushes upfield avoiding Dolphins defensive lineman Keith Cooper Jr. (97) during the Miami Dolphins preseason game versus the Washington Commanders at Northwest Stadium on August 14, 2026, in Landover, MD. (Photo by Lee Coleman/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Daily Slop – 17 August 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Just around the corner pic.twitter.com/IvrCforbGS — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) August 16, 2026 Articles Bullock’s Film Room (subscription) Commanders Film Review: Sonny Styles vs Dolphins Sonny Styles made his NFL debut in the Commanders preseason opener against the Dolphins on Friday night. The seventh overall pick started the game but played just one series before being held out for the rest of the game. In that series, the Commanders defense struggled to stop the Dolphins as Miami drove 93 yards down the field on a 14-play touchdown drive. Some fans have been quick to jump on Styles and be extremely critical of his performance, which is obviously silly given the context. But as such, I thought I’d take a closer look at how Styles played. Run Game In the run game, Styles had a few ups and downs but was largely pretty solid. There were a few plays I saw people online being critical of when actually Styles did exactly what he was meant to do. [The analysis below refers to the FOURTH snap shown in this tweet] Sonny Styles Every Snap From His NFL Debut pic.twitter.com/Na247BDJb1 — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) August 15, 2026 This was one of the Dolphins first runs of the game. They call an outside zone run to the right. The Commanders call a run stunt, with defensive lineman Johnny Newton and Ricky Barber both stunting to the left side of the line in order to cause disruption to the blocking scheme. With those lineman stunting inside, the linebackers behind them have to fill the gaps vacated by the lineman up front. Johnny Newton starts lined up on the outside shoulder of the right guard, which would typically mean he’s responsible for the B gap between the right guard and right tackle, but as he stunts inside towards the center, someone else needs to fill that B gap. That’s where Styles comes in. Styles is the linebacker to that side. His job is to fill the B gap vacated by Newton’s stunt. Then Leo Chenal has to work across from the back side to help fill in behind Styles. Styles attacks the B gap at the snap and fills his assignment. The right guard peels off his block on Newton and works across just in time to pick up Styles, which enables the running back to cut his run back inside behind Styles and the right guard. But that means the run hits in the A gap, which isn’t Styles’ responsibility. He did his job filling the B gap and forcing the back to cut his run inside towards the rest of the defense. Unfortunately, Newton gets caught up on the center. Dolphins center Aaron Brewer is one of the best centers in the league and he manages to keep Newton engaged just long enough to open that A gap for the running back. Chenal does his best to try and get across to fill that A gap from the back side, but left tackle Patrick Paul works down the line and manages to push Chenal out of the gap as the back runs through it. That’s what enables the back to break through the line of scrimmage and into the secondary for a nice gain. But for Styles, he did his job just fine, so this one isn’t on him. Lots of talk on here yesterday about Sonny Styles' performance in the Commanders preseason opener, so I figured I'd take a closer look and break it down: https://t.co/yDAIe2bxd3 pic.twitter.com/GFWFJboc7l — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) August 16, 2026 Bullock’s Film Room (subscription) Commanders Film Review: Brandon Coleman vs Dolphins On Friday night, the Commanders had their preseason opener against the Dolphins and while most of their starters rested, Coleman played alongside Paul for the first few series. He only played 12 snaps total, which is obviously a small sample size, but there were signs of encouragement there. [The analysis below refers to the play embedded in this tweet] Brandon Coleman only played a couple of series in the Commanders preseason opener against the Dolphins, but in those series he showed some encouraging signs. I broke down his performance: https://t.co/fVRcwKPhNh pic.twitter.com/5eFEfX9lao — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) August 17, 2026 On this play, Coleman faces Dolphins edge rusher Chop Robinson, a first round pick back in 2024 with excellent speed and ability to dip and bend around the corner. Robinson takes a wide alignment pre-snap, trying to give himself the best possible angle of attack. At the snap, Coleman closes off that angle with two smooth but quick kicksteps that gain good width and depth. With Coleman able to take away the speed rush thanks to his quick feet, Robinson has to attempt something else. Robinson attempts a stutter move. In his rookie year, Coleman may have fallen for this and lunged at the defender, but here he shows much more patience. He lets Robinson come to him and then strikes with a strong punch to Robinson’s outside shoulder at the perfect time. That punch stuns Robinson for a beat and takes away his path to the edge. Robinson brings up his own hand to try and swipe Coleman’s hand down, but Coleman shows good hand strength to keep himself attached. If I’m being nitpicky, Coleman is a little off-balance here. If you pause the clip as Robinson swipes with his outside hand on Coleman’s outside hand, you can see Coleman is reaching just slightly as his feet are still gaining depth while his hands stay engaged. Ideally he’d keep his feet under him a bit more to maintain a more powerful position, but he still has enough power to gain control of this block. Robinson then closes the gap and tries to convert to power, but Coleman has all the leverage and wins the rep comfortably. Those stutter moves were often issues for Coleman in his rookie year because he was so eager to strike with his hands and initiate contact with the defender that he would end up lunging and losing balance. But he displayed a few times in this game he could be more patient, even against those stutter moves. Quick Reader Survey The Athletic (paywall) Commanders QB Marcus Mariota sprains MCL, will likely miss rest of preseason: Sources Washington Commanders quarterback Marcus Mariota sprained his MCL in the team’s preseason win over the Miami Dolphins on Friday, according to two league sources who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly on the matter. Although his timetable for return is not yet clear, he is likely done for the rest of preseason, at least. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Last Man Standig (paywall) Why Marcus Mariota is more indispensable than Washington would like It’s not that Mariota’s talent level at 32 is particularly singular. It’s that he has shown a knack for giving Washington’s offense at least a puncher’s chance whenever Daniels is unavailable. It’s unclear whether the other two reserve quarterbacks, Athan Kaliakmanis and Sam Hartman, can even throw a jab at the NFL level. Going with 39-year-old Josh Johnson for the final two games in 2025, with Washington long ago eliminated from the playoffs, spoke volumes about the staff’s view of Hartman as an on-field consideration. Entering his third season, Hartman has shown little reason to think that view has changed. Quinn said there is no plan to add another quarterback in the interim. Maybe Mariota is indeed ready for Week 1. Maybe…

title: Joshua Josephs and the legend of Andrew Van Ginkel
summary: Ever since Daronte Jones was hired as the new defensive coordinator for the Commanders in January, Washington fans have heard about the “Van Ginkel” role. A fifth-round selection of the Miami Dolphins in the 2019 NFL Draft, Andrew Van Ginkel started his career in relative anonymity, providing good, if not spectacular, production for the Miami […]
full_text: Ever since Daronte Jones was hired as the new defensive coordinator for the Commanders in January, Washington fans have heard about the “Van Ginkel” role. A fifth-round selection of the Miami Dolphins in the 2019 NFL Draft, Andrew Van Ginkel started his career in relative anonymity, providing good, if not spectacular, production for the Miami Dolphins. The head coach that drafted him? None other than current Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores. Flores was an early believer in Van Ginkel’s potential, and he jumped at the opportunity to sign the outside linebacker when he became available in 2024. Flores took Andrew’s length, instincts, and versatility and used him to create a constant unknown for quarterbacks and offensive coordinators. At times Andrew Van Ginkel will rush, other times he will drop in coverage, and still others set the edge versus the run. While not dominant as a pass rusher, Van Ginkel has a good first step and the athleticism to create havoc on the outside. After spending multiple years in Flores’ system, he has a firm grasp of the defensive concepts and how to execute the scheme. It makes for a key cog in Minnesota’s defense, and at one point last season it was noted the Vikings ranked eighth in total defense with Van Ginkel in the lineup and 20th without him. In fact, Andrew Van Ginkel’s instincts and effectiveness are so good that descriptions of his play sometimes almost take on mythical qualities. Consider this write-up on Van Ginkel by The Athletic’s Alec Lewis: There are instances where Van Ginkel, 30, seems to teleport. In other moments, a review of a Vikings defensive coverage is almost necessary to ascertain whether there are multiple Van Ginkels on the field. His ability to make plays in both coverage and in pass rush is so rare that some might, if you will pardon the expression, consider him a unicorn amongst defensive edge players. NFL Top 100 Players of 2025: @Vikings LB Andrew Van Ginkel earns the No. 88 spot! @NFLFilms pic.twitter.com/K24EblLTAO — NFL (@NFL) July 8, 2025 So which options do the Washington Commanders have for this key role in Jones’ defense? The first, and most likely, is K’Lavon Chaisson. The projected starter opposite Odafe Oweh, Chaisson has plenty of pass rush ability and streaky ability to set the edge in the run game but is not comparable to Van Ginkel in coverage. Gink played the most coverage snaps of any edge in the league last year, with 135 coverage snaps. Chaisson played about 25 coverage snaps with the Patriots last season, and it has never really been part of his six-year career. Leo Chenal might also be under consideration, but he has limited ability as a pass rusher, and his coverage skills are still a work in progress. The most natural fit for Van Ginkel’s role on the Commanders’ roster may be a fifth-round selection of their own. Joshua Josephs was selected with the No. 147 overall pick in this year’s NFL Draft. A four-year senior out of Tennessee, the selection caught some fans by surprise, but Josephs offers upside as a long, athletic edge and was the top player on Adam Peters’ board by a wide margin at the time of the selection. A bit undersized, Josephs is almost a physical mirror image of Van Ginkel and his athletic profile is similar as well. Very interesting comp from @LoganPaulsenNFL between Andrew Van Ginkle & Commanders 5th rd pick Joshua Josephs. The measurables are there, JJ has longer arms, draft position almost identical. AVG has killed Washington over the years. Something to file away pic.twitter.com/n1mAHw8I14 — JP Finlay (@JPFinlayNBCS) April 27, 2026 Like Van Ginkel, Josephs has a good first step and plays with effort and a high motor. Playing behind James Pearce for a good part of his college career, Josephs had limited production in college but a good final season with the Volunteers, recording 33 tackles, six TFLs, four sacks, three pass deflections, and three forced fumbles. Josephs plays with discipline and gap integrity when setting the edge but can be inconsistent as a tackler and needs to add strength. While this may make him seem like any other developmental Day 3 edge prospect, the interesting part of Josephs’ training camp has been his ability in coverage. While Josh wasn’t known for his coverage skills at Tennessee, he has performed well when called upon. His draft profile from the Ringer cites, “Josephs shows the fluidity and athleticism to flip his hips and drop back into coverage.” So far that has proven to be true, and the rookie has looked comfortable dropping into space during training camp. Forget Sonny for a second, do y’all see how fluid Joshua Josephs looks when dropping? In that 48 jersey that you can’t miss? pic.twitter.com/OGqTzmeeB9 — Full Command (@FullCommandShow) May 9, 2026 I am SPEECHLESS at what preseason is gonna look like, that man read that perfectly! he flip his hips one second early thats a pick😮‍💨 pic.twitter.com/oILWSBQKGH — Ben Sinnott #1 Fan (@commanderhub) August 3, 2026 Josephs has been catching the eye of reporters in training camp all summer and had a great joint practice session with Miami. While he didn’t have any splash plays in Friday night’s preseason game and his lack of a pass rush plan was evident, Josephs’ energy and motor were on display. His length stands out of the field, and he was utilized in Van Ginkel’s role on several occasions. While he did allow a completion, Josh looked capable in coverage on the play. Joshua Josephs is having a FIELD DAY! Multiple sacks and pressures ‼️ — On The Fence Podcast (@theotfpodcast) August 12, 2026 #Commanders rookie EDGE Joshua Josephs looked great vs the Dolphins Had some very good reps and brought a noticeable amount of pressure. He’s a guy to watch and imaginably, he’ll continue to develop and gain a bigger role. #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/6Dw2vgrnw0 — brandon (@JayDanielsMVP) August 16, 2026 Josephs still lacks Van Ginkel’s instincts and innate ability to read defenses, but the tools are there. He needs time to develop his game, but the early indications are Josh is ahead of schedule. Daronte Jones has noticed and believes that he is in a good situation to continue his upward trajectory. “Josh is, he’s picking up the tutelage of Coach Pagano. But then also, he’s surrounded by some good guys in that room. With K’Lavon Chaisson and ‘Doff’ [OLB Odafe Oweh] and Dorance [Armstrong], they’re in his ear. He’s watching those guys, he’s learning from those guys. So, he’s in a good group where he can kind of fast track a little bit some of the maturation process, but I like where he is so far. It all adds up to a breakout performance for the rookie coming sooner than later, and fans should expect Josephs to take on a rotational role in the Washington Commanders’ defense at some point during the season. Rotational doesn’t necessarily mean insignificant, because, as Andrew Van Ginkel has shown, the ability to disguise the coverage while generating pressure makes a Flores’ style defense far more effective. Hopefully Josephs can do the same for Daronte Jones and the Washington Commanders. Quick Reader Survey
author: John Portis

title: NFL Future Power Rankings: 2027-29 projections for 32 teams
summary: How might all 32 NFL franchises stack up beyond 2026? Our forward-looking ranking factors in each team's future QB, roster, front office and coaching situations.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL season kicks off in less than a month, and we'll have plenty of coverage about the race to Super Bowl LXI in Los Angeles. But we're also in the business of trying to predict the future.

 In our annual Future Power Rankings, we're not focused on the outcome of this season. Instead, we're ranking all 32 teams by who is primed to be among the league's best from the 2027 through 2029 seasons.

 To do so, we asked our panel of experts -- analysts Louis Riddick, Aaron Schatz, Ben Solak and Seth Walder -- to rate each team's quarterback situation, remaining (non-QB) roster makeup, front office and coaching staff using this scale:

 
 100: A+ (elite) 
 90-99: A (great) 
 80-89: B (very good) 
 70-79: C (average) 
 51-69: D (very bad) 
 50 and below: F (disastrous) 
 
 After averaging the results from the panelists, each of the four categories was weighted to create the overall score: quarterback (20%), roster (30%), front office (25%) and coaching (25%). The result is a comprehensive ranking based on how well each team is positioned for the future. Our experts then picked out reasons for optimism, reasons to worry, crucial stats/nuggets to know and bold predictions for all 32 franchises over that three-year span.

 

 Jump to a team: 
 ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN 
 CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND 
 JAX | KC | LV | LAC | LAR | MIA | MIN 
 NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF 
 SEA | TB | TEN | WSH 

 Note: Overall scores are rounded to the nearest 10th of a point. 

 

 

 1. Seattle Seahawks (Overall score: 88.7) 
 

 Reason for hope:  The league has been looking for a young defensive counterstrike to the ascent of offensive masterminds Sean McVay and Kyle Shanahan, and the Seahawks have finally found it! Coach Mike Macdonald has a stellar track record of defensive player development, and the emergence of WR Jaxon Smith-Njigba , OT Charles Cross and QB Sam Darnold sets a high floor in Seattle for years to come.  -- Solak 

 Reason for concern:  The relationship between Darnold and former OC Klint Kubiak was an obvious net positive for the organization. For the future, what does that real-time relationship look like between Darnold and new OC Brian Fleury? Fleury is not just calling plays for the first time on the NFL level but also doing it with a roster that is set up to contend into the future.  -- Riddick 

 Nugget to know:  Including the postseason, the 2025 Seahawks finished with the highest DVOA of any team since the 2007 Patriots. The top-12 teams by DVOA since 2010 finished with an average of 10.9 wins the following season (prorated for a 17-game season). However, these numbers are dragged down by two injury-riddled 49ers teams (2020 and 2024). Remove those teams, and the average is 11.9 wins.  -- Schatz 

 Bold prediction for 2027-29:  Darnold will not be on the Seahawks in 2028. He started last season red-hot and finished fairly strong in Seattle's Super Bowl run. But from Weeks 10 to 18, he ranked 27th out of 30 quarterbacks in QBR. The Super Bowl win certainly will buy Darnold time. But if he stumbles in 2027, I don't think there are guarantees that he will be re-signed .  -- Walder 

 

 
 

 2. Philadelphia Eagles  (Overall score: 88.1) 
 

 Reason for hope:  Even in an offseason of tumult, with A.J. Brown traded and the transition to a new offensive system, the Eagles rank very highly in our future outlook. Why? Because general manager Howie Roseman has proved over the past decade that nobody builds contenders more quickly. The Eagles' star-studded young defense is proof alone.   -- Solak 

 Reason for concern:  Decision-makers in Philadelphia clearly believed the offense needed to evolve philosophically, and the change was made to bring in offensive coordinator Sean Mannion. His ability to teach, develop and use the skills of QB Jalen Hurts -- without fully neutralizing what has made him a Super Bowl-winning QB -- will shape this organization over the next several years.  -- Riddick 

 Nugget to know:  The Eagles project to have the league's youngest defense if we look at their top-12 projected defensive players (starters in both base and nickel). The average age is 25.6; Jonathan Greenard and Zack Baun are their only starters over 27.   -- Schatz 

 Bold prediction for 2027-29:  The Eagles will trade Jalyx Hunt or  Nolan Smith Jr . ahead of the 2027 season. They will be entering the final year of their deals and are the second- or third-best pass rusher on the Eagles, in some order, with Greenard aboard. Trading either player could net Philadelphia draft capital going forward -- and save some money if it's Smith.  -- Walder 

 

 
 

 3. Detroit Lions  (Overall score: 86.2) 
 

 Reason for hope:  As GM Brad Holmes begins paying the legendary 2023 draft class that galvanized this Lions turnaround, future contention becomes tougher and tougher in Detroit. But between Holmes and coach Dan Campbell, the Lions' leadership is unquestionable. And Detroit's group of young stars entering their primes (RB  Jahmyr Gibbs , LB  Jack Campbell , OT  Penei Sewell  and WR Amon-Ra St. Brown ) is as deep as any.  -- Solak 

 Reason for concern:  I still have concerns about the Lions' ability to rush the passer at a championship level (26th in pass rush win rate last season), although rookie 2026 second-round pick Derrick Moore could lessen some of the burden on Aidan Hutchinson . What is of more concern is the secondary, where  Brian Branch is trying to come back from an Achilles tear  and Kerby Joseph is rehabbing a knee injury . Both are among the best in the league at their position, so it would be a major blow if they can't get back to their top form.   -- Riddick 

 Nugget to know:  Detroit has reset its offensive line with youth, and only Miami now has a younger average age among its five projected starters for the 2026 season. The Lions' starting linemen range in age from right tackle Blake Miller (22) to center Juice Scruggs (26), who replaces the injured Cade Mays (27).  -- Schatz 

 Bold prediction for 2027-29:  Hutchinson will win Defensive Player of the Year. His five pre-injury games in 2024 always stick out in my mind, when he had 7.5 sacks and an obscene 35.0% pass rush win rate at edge ( Danielle Hunter led qualifiers that year at 26.1%). Of course, that was a small sample. But Hutchinson has the capability to be an elite -- even the best -- edge rusher over a whole season.  -- Walder 

 

 
 

 4. Denver Broncos  (Overall score: 85.6) 
 

 Reason for hope:  Across the 53-man roster, there is perhaps no team deeper than Denver. And the Broncos' coaching staff, with Sean Payton and Vance Joseph, features two of the league's preeminent schemers over the past decade. The continued growth of QB  Bo Nix  and the final addition of WR  Jaylen Waddle could push this team into one of the three Super Bowl matchups in question.  -- Solak 

 Reason for concern:  Last year , I expressed my concern about whether Denver's RB room could make this offense complete. I'm not as worried about that now, as I think the addition of fourth-rounder Jonah Coleman (an absolute tank ) next to RJ Harvey gives the Broncos the perfect 1-2 punch over the next few years. My concern now is whether new coordinator Davis Webb can create a balanced offense to go along with their lights-out defense.   -- Riddick 

 Nugget to know:  The Broncos are set up well for the future, but age on the offensive line is an issue. Starters range in age from Quinn Meinerz (28) to Garett Bolles (34). Guard Kage Casey , a 2026 fourth-round pick, is the only offensive lineman Denver has selected in the past two drafts.  -- Schatz 

 Bold prediction for 2027-29: Ja'Quan McMillian will become the highest-paid nickel back in 2027 -- with Denver or another team. McMillian is an excellent slot corner on a good defense, allowing 1.0 yards per coverage snap (average) and minus-19 expected points added on targets (fourth best).
